Task board: Platform 2026.2 project.

docs.title: The project
docs.text:
A microservices platform for a store: the user signs up, logs in and looks up exchange rates between currencies. Every request comes in through a single entry point (the gateway, behind an Nginx load balancer), which validates the JWT token and forwards the user's identity to the services.

flowchart LR
    internet([Internet]) e0@==> lb["lb · Nginx"]
    subgraph trusted [Trusted layer]
        lb e1@==> gw["gateway<br/>(replicas)"]
        gw --> auth
        gw --> account
        gw --> exchange
        gw <-->|token → id| redis[(Redis)]
        auth --> account
        account --> db[(PostgreSQL)]
        account -.->|event| kafka[[Kafka]] -.-> notification
    end
    exchange --> api3([Exchange rate API])
    e0@{ animate: true }
    e1@{ animate: true }

Details in Architecture.

docs.title: How the video was made
docs.text: The scenes from this documentation's pages were recorded with Playwright (an automated browser, with the caption placed on the page itself); the EKS demo uses only HTTP through the public ELB, like any regular user, with the JWT and the demo account's password hidden on screen. ffmpeg stitches the scenes into an MP4 (H.264, 1280×720).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    user([User]) e0@==>|":8080 local / ELB on AWS"| lb
    subgraph lbl [Load balancing]
        lb["lb · Nginx"]:::orange
    end
    subgraph trusted [Trusted layer — no exposed port]
        lb e1@==> gw1["gateway 1"]
        lb e2@==> gw2["gateway 2"]
        gw1 & gw2 <-->|"token → id-account"| redis[("Redis<br/>cache")]:::red
        gw1 & gw2 -->|"/auth/**"| auth
        gw1 & gw2 -->|"/accounts/**"| account
        gw1 & gw2 -->|"/exchange/**"| exchange
        auth -->|Feign| account
        account --> db[("PostgreSQL")]
        account -.->|"AccountCreated (outbox)"| kafka[["Kafka"]]:::red
        kafka -.-> notification
        notification -.->|SMTP| mailpit(["Mailpit"])
    end
    exchange --> ext([External exchange rate API])
    e0@{ animate: true }
    e1@{ animate: true }
    e2@{ animate: true }
    classDef orange fill:#FCBE3E
    classDef red fill:#fcc
Component Technology Role lb Nginx Single exposed entry point. Distributes requests across the gateway replicas. gateway Spring Cloud Gateway (WebFlux) Routes, validates the JWT (via Auth), and injects the id-account header. redis Redis 7 Cache shared across the gateway replicas: token → account id. auth Spring Boot + JJWT Login, JWT issuing and validation. account Spring Boot + JPA + Flyway Sign-up and account data. exchange Python Currency exchange rates (third-party API). db PostgreSQL 17 Database for Account (schema accounts) and Notification (schema notification). kafka Apache Kafka 4 (KRaft) Messaging: account-events topic (see Messaging). notification Spring Boot + Spring Kafka Consumes AccountCreated and sends the welcome email (idempotent, with DLT). mailpit Mailpit Fake SMTP server with a web inbox (local/cluster only).

docs.title: Flow of an authenticated request
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor U as User
    participant LB as Nginx
    participant GW as Gateway
    participant R as Redis
    participant A as Auth
    participant S as Service (account/exchange)
    U->>LB: GET /accounts (cookie __store_jwt_token)
    LB->>GW: proxy (round robin across replicas)
    GW->>GW: strips id-account sent by the client
    GW->>R: GET gateway:token:sha256(jwt)
    alt cache hit
        R-->>GW: account id
    else cache miss
        GW->>A: POST /auth/solve {token}
        A-->>GW: {idAccount} or 401
        GW->>R: SET ... EX min(5 min, JWT exp)
    end
    GW->>S: GET /accounts + id-account header
    S-->>U: response

docs.title: API contract
docs.text: Agreed upon within the group (based on the course website, hands-on 1 and 3, and the Exchange exercise).

docs.title: Gateway
docs.text:
• Reads the __store_jwt_token cookie on every request.
  • Open routes (no token): POST /auth/register, POST /auth/login, GET /auth/logout.
  • Everything else (including /accounts/** and /exchange/**) requires a token.
  • Validates it by calling POST /auth/solve on Auth and forwards the id in the id-account header.
  • /exchanges/** is also accepted and rewritten to /exchange/** (the assignment uses both names).

docs.title: Auth (http://auth:8080)
docs.text: Method Route Input Output POST /auth/register { name, email, password } 200 POST /auth/login { email, password } 200 + Set-Cookie: __store_jwt_token=<jwt> GET /auth/logout — 200, clears the cookie GET /auth/me id-account header { id, name, email } POST /auth/solve { token } { idAccount } (internal, only the gateway calls it) GET /auth/health-check — 200

docs.title: JWT
docs.text:
• Claims: jti = account id, sub = name, email, iss, nbf, exp.
  • Lifetime: 24 h (JWT_DURATION). Secret in JWT_SECRET_KEY (environment variable, never in the code).
  • Cookie: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=None, Path=/.

docs.title: Account (http://account:8080)
docs.text: Method Route Input Output POST /accounts { name, email, password } 201 GET /accounts — [{ id, name, email }] GET /accounts/{id} — { id, name, email } DELETE /accounts/{id} — 204 POST /accounts/login { email, password } { id, name, email } (internal, Auth calls it) GET /accounts/health-check — 200

docs.title: Exchange (Python)
docs.text: Method Route Input Output GET /exchange/{from}/{to} id-account header { sell, buy, date, id-account }

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text: Decision Reason Service names auth, account, exchange, gateway are the same in compose and k8s The Feign clients use http://account:8080 and http://auth:8080. Only lb publishes a port The gateway and the services stay in the trusted layer; the id-account header can only come from the gateway. Token cache in Redis, key = SHA-256 of the JWT Takes Auth out of the path of every request without storing the token in plain text. One image per service on GHCR and ECR (via OIDC, no AWS key on GitHub) The pipeline publishes multi-arch images (amd64 for EKS, arm64 for the group's Macs).

docs.title: HTTPS (known limitation)
docs.text:
Auth returns the token in the __store_jwt_token cookie with HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite=None. The browser only stores a Secure cookie that comes from HTTPS (or from localhost), so:

Where Status Local compose (http://localhost) Works in the browser: localhost counts as a secure origin. EKS (http://<elb>.elb.amazonaws.com) The ELB serves HTTP only. Clients that send the cookie in the header (curl, scripts/smoke-test.sh, k6) work; the browser discards the cookie and the protected routes return 401.

Why there is no HTTPS on EKS: a public ACM certificate requires a DNS-validated domain, and the group has no domain; the ELB name belongs to AWS and changes every time the cluster is recreated. A self-signed certificate on Nginx would make the browser show a security warning, which is unacceptable for a store.

What it would look like in production: a custom domain + an ACM certificate + TLS terminated at the load balancer, with annotations on the lb Service and an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect:

metadata:
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-ssl-cert: arn:aws:acm:us-east-2:<conta>:certificate/<id>
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-ssl-ports: "443"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-backend-protocol: http

From the load balancer inward, traffic stays on HTTP, inside the cluster's private network (trusted layer).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Git, Java 25, and Maven 3.9+
  • Docker with Docker Compose v2

docs.title: Locally (Docker Compose)
docs.text:
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/pna26/platform.git
cd platform

./scripts/build.sh            # mvn install das interfaces + mvn package dos serviços + cria o .env
docker compose up -d --build  # sobe db, redis, account, auth, exchange, gateway (2 réplicas) e lb
./scripts/smoke-test.sh       # teste ponta a ponta

The platform is available at http://localhost:8080. Only lb (Nginx) publishes a port; the other services stay on the compose internal network. Grafana (http://localhost:3000) and Prometheus (:9090) are bound to 127.0.0.1 — see Observability.

compose.yaml
# Plataforma completa rodando localmente.
#   ./scripts/build.sh            # compila os jars (interfaces + serviços)
#   docker compose up -d --build  # sobe tudo; entrada em http://localhost:8080
#
# Só o lb (Nginx) publica porta para fora: gateway, auth, account, exchange,
# redis e db ficam na rede interna do compose (camada confiável). Prometheus
# (9090), Grafana (3000), Kafka UI (8089) e Mailpit (8025) ficam presos ao
# 127.0.0.1 da máquina.

name: store

services:

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${DB_USER:-store}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-store}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${DB_NAME:-store}
    volumes:
      - db_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: [ "CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U $${POSTGRES_USER} -d $${POSTGRES_DB}" ]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 20

  # Bottleneck: cache. Guarda token -> id da conta para o gateway não chamar
  # o Auth em toda requisição (ver api/gateway-service/.../TokenCache.java)
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    command: redis-server --appendonly yes
    volumes:
      - redis_data:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: [ "CMD", "redis-cli", "ping" ]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 20

  account:
    build:
      context: ./api/account-service
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    environment:
      DATABASE_HOST: db
      DATABASE_PORT: 5432
      DATABASE_DB: ${DB_NAME:-store}
      DATABASE_USERNAME: ${DB_USER:-store}
      DATABASE_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-store}
      KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS: kafka:9092
    deploy:
      replicas: 1
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      kafka-init:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

  auth:
    build:
      context: ./api/auth-service
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    environment:
      # segredo vem do .env (scripts/build.sh gera um aleatório); nunca no código
      JWT_SECRET_KEY: ${JWT_SECRET_KEY:?defina JWT_SECRET_KEY no .env (veja .env.example)}
      JWT_DURATION: ${JWT_DURATION:-86400000}
    deploy:
      replicas: 1
    depends_on:
      - account

  gateway:
    build:
      context: ./api/gateway-service
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    environment:
      REDIS_HOST: redis
      REDIS_PORT: 6379
      # liga/desliga o cache do token (para comparar no teste de carga)
      TOKEN_CACHE_ENABLED: ${TOKEN_CACHE_ENABLED:-true}
      CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS: ${CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS:-http://localhost,http://localhost:3000,http://localhost:8080}
    # sem "ports": só é alcançável pelo lb
    deploy:
      replicas: ${GATEWAY_REPLICAS:-2}
    depends_on:
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
      auth:
        condition: service_started
      account:
        condition: service_started

  # Bottleneck: balanceamento de carga (Nginx na frente das réplicas do gateway)
  lb:
    image: nginx:1.29-alpine
    ports:
      - "${LB_PORT:-8080}:80"
    volumes:
      - ./setup/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
    depends_on:
      - gateway

  # Exchange (Python/FastAPI). Cotação da AwesomeAPI com cache em memória
  # (bottleneck: ver docs/bottlenecks/exchange-cache.md)
  exchange:
    build:
      context: ./api/exchange-service
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    environment:
      CACHE_TTL: ${EXCHANGE_CACHE_TTL:-30}
      EXCHANGE_API_TOKEN: ${EXCHANGE_API_TOKEN:-}
    deploy:
      replicas: ${EXCHANGE_REPLICAS:-1}

  # Bottleneck: mensageria (docs/bottlenecks/messaging.md), como no Hands-on 7.
  # O account grava a conta e o evento AccountCreated na mesma transação
  # (outbox) e um relay publica no tópico account-events; o notification
  # consome, deduplica pelo eventId e manda o e-mail de boas-vindas ao Mailpit.
  # Kafka 4 de um nó em modo KRaft (broker e controlador no mesmo processo).
  # Só a rede interna do compose fala com ele (sem porta publicada).
  kafka:
    image: apache/kafka:4.3.1
    hostname: kafka
    environment:
      KAFKA_NODE_ID: 1
      KAFKA_PROCESS_ROLES: broker,controller
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_QUORUM_VOTERS: 1@kafka:9093
      KAFKA_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://:9092,CONTROLLER://:9093
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://kafka:9092
      KAFKA_LISTENER_SECURITY_PROTOCOL_MAP: PLAINTEXT:PLAINTEXT,CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_LISTENER_NAMES: CONTROLLER
      KAFKA_INTER_BROKER_LISTENER_NAME: PLAINTEXT
      KAFKA_OFFSETS_TOPIC_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_MIN_ISR: 1
      KAFKA_GROUP_INITIAL_REBALANCE_DELAY_MS: 0
      # tópicos criados explicitamente pelo kafka-init (o automático teria 1 partição)
      KAFKA_AUTO_CREATE_TOPICS_ENABLE: "false"
      KAFKA_LOG_DIRS: /var/lib/kafka/data
    volumes:
      - kafka_data:/var/lib/kafka/data
    healthcheck:
      test: [ "CMD-SHELL", "/opt/kafka/bin/kafka-broker-api-versions.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 > /dev/null 2>&1" ]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 10s
      start_period: 60s
      retries: 20

  # tarefa única: cria os tópicos e termina. A DLT tem as mesmas 6 partições
  # (o Spring publica a mensagem que falhou no mesmo número de partição)
  kafka-init:
    image: apache/kafka:4.3.1
    depends_on:
      kafka:
        condition: service_healthy
    entrypoint: [ "/bin/sh", "-c" ]
    command:
      - |
        /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --create --if-not-exists           --topic account-events --partitions 6 --replication-factor 1 &&
        /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --create --if-not-exists           --topic account-events-dlt --partitions 6 --replication-factor 1
    restart: "no"

  kafka-ui:
    image: kafbat/kafka-ui:v1.5.0
    environment:
      KAFKA_CLUSTERS_0_NAME: store
      KAFKA_CLUSTERS_0_BOOTSTRAPSERVERS: kafka:9092
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:${KAFKA_UI_PORT:-8089}:8080"
    depends_on:
      kafka:
        condition: service_healthy

  # provedor de e-mail falso (SMTP 1025 na rede interna, caixa de entrada web)
  mailpit:
    image: axllent/mailpit:v1.31
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:${MAILPIT_PORT:-8025}:8025"

  notification:
    build:
      context: ./api/notification-service
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    environment:
      DATABASE_HOST: db
      DATABASE_PORT: 5432
      DATABASE_DB: ${DB_NAME:-store}
      DATABASE_USERNAME: ${DB_USER:-store}
      DATABASE_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-store}
      KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS: kafka:9092
      MAIL_HOST: mailpit
      NOTIFY_CONCURRENCY: ${NOTIFY_CONCURRENCY:-3}   # threads consumidoras (no máximo 6 úteis: 6 partições)
      EMAIL_LATENCY: ${EMAIL_LATENCY:-50ms}          # latência simulada do provedor de e-mail
      NOTIFY_IDEMPOTENT: ${NOTIFY_IDEMPOTENT:-true}  # false = sem deduplicação (para ver duplicatas)
    deploy:
      replicas: 1
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      mailpit:
        condition: service_started
      kafka-init:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

  # Bottleneck: observabilidade (docs/bottlenecks/observability.md).
  # Portas só no 127.0.0.1 do host: ferramentas de operação, não da loja.
  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:v3.5.0
    command:
      - --config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
      - --storage.tsdb.retention.time=7d
      # o k6 (scripts/load-test.sh) envia as métricas do teste por remote write
      - --web.enable-remote-write-receiver
    volumes:
      - ./setup/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro
      - prometheus_data:/prometheus
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:${PROMETHEUS_PORT:-9090}:9090"
    depends_on:
      - gateway
      - exchange

  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:12.1.0
    environment:
      PROMETHEUS_URL: http://prometheus:9090
      GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD: ${GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD:-admin}
      GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_ENABLED: "false"
      GF_DASHBOARDS_DEFAULT_HOME_DASHBOARD_PATH: /var/lib/grafana/dashboards/store.json
      GF_ANALYTICS_REPORTING_ENABLED: "false"
    volumes:
      - ./setup/grafana/provisioning:/etc/grafana/provisioning:ro
      - ./setup/grafana/dashboards:/var/lib/grafana/dashboards:ro
      - grafana_data:/var/lib/grafana
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:${GRAFANA_PORT:-3000}:3000"
    depends_on:
      - prometheus

volumes:
  db_data:
  kafka_data:
  redis_data:
  prometheus_data:
  grafana_data:

The .env file is created by scripts/build.sh from .env.example, with a random JWT_SECRET_KEY (openssl rand -base64 32). It never goes into git.

docs.title: Usage example
docs.text:
# cadastro e login (o cookie fica no arquivo cookies.txt)
curl -X POST localhost:8080/auth/register -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Ana","email":"ana@store.com","password":"123456"}'
curl -c cookies.txt -X POST localhost:8080/auth/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"ana@store.com","password":"123456"}'

# rotas protegidas (o curl só reenvia cookie Secure em HTTPS, então mandamos o header)
TOKEN=$(awk '/__store_jwt_token/ {print $7}' cookies.txt)
curl -H "Cookie: __store_jwt_token=$TOKEN" localhost:8080/auth/me
curl -H "Cookie: __store_jwt_token=$TOKEN" localhost:8080/accounts

docs.title: Smoke test
docs.text:
scripts/smoke-test.sh is the same script that runs in CI (integration workflow). It checks:

  • sign-up, login (HttpOnly cookie), /auth/me, /accounts, /exchange/USD/BRL, and logout;
  • 401 without a token, with an invalid token, and with a forged id-account;
  • that at least 2 gateway replicas responded (load balancing);
  • that the token was cached in Redis;
  • that /gateway/actuator/prometheus is not exposed through lb.
scripts/smoke-test.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Teste ponta a ponta da plataforma rodando (compose local ou EKS):
#   ./scripts/smoke-test.sh                       # http://localhost:8080
#   BASE_URL=http://<elb-da-aws> ./scripts/smoke-test.sh
# Confere o contrato da API, o 401 sem token, o header id-account forjado,
# o balanceamento entre réplicas e o cache do token no Redis.
set -euo pipefail

BASE_URL="${BASE_URL:-http://localhost:8080}"
EMAIL="smoke+$(date +%s)$RANDOM@store.test"
PASS="senha-forte-123"
fail() { echo "FALHOU: $*" >&2; exit 1; }
ok() { echo "ok  - $*"; }
status() { curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "$@"; }

echo ">> esperando o gateway em $BASE_URL"
for i in $(seq 1 60); do
  [ "$(status "$BASE_URL/health-check")" = "200" ] && break
  sleep 2
  [ "$i" = 60 ] && fail "gateway não respondeu"
done
ok "gateway no ar"

# o auth/account podem demorar um pouco mais que o gateway para subir
for i in $(seq 1 60); do
  code=$(status -X POST "$BASE_URL/auth/register" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d "{\"name\":\"Smoke Test\",\"email\":\"$EMAIL\",\"password\":\"$PASS\"}")
  case "$code" in 200|201) break ;; esac
  sleep 3
  [ "$i" = 60 ] && fail "POST /auth/register respondeu $code"
done
ok "POST /auth/register ($code)"

headers=$(curl -s -D - -o /dev/null -X POST "$BASE_URL/auth/login" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"email\":\"$EMAIL\",\"password\":\"$PASS\"}")
echo "$headers" | head -1 | grep -q ' 200' || fail "POST /auth/login: $(echo "$headers" | head -1)"
TOKEN=$(echo "$headers" | tr -d '\r' | sed -n 's/^[Ss]et-[Cc]ookie: __store_jwt_token=\([^;]*\).*/\1/p' | head -1)
[ -n "$TOKEN" ] || fail "login não devolveu o cookie __store_jwt_token"
echo "$headers" | grep -qi 'set-cookie:.*HttpOnly' || fail "cookie sem HttpOnly"
ok "POST /auth/login devolveu o cookie __store_jwt_token (HttpOnly)"

COOKIE="Cookie: __store_jwt_token=$TOKEN"

[ "$(status "$BASE_URL/accounts")" = "401" ] || fail "GET /accounts sem token deveria ser 401"
ok "GET /accounts sem token -> 401"

[ "$(status -H 'id-account: forjado' "$BASE_URL/accounts")" = "401" ] || fail "id-account forjado abriu a rota"
ok "header id-account forjado sem token -> 401"

[ "$(status -H "Cookie: __store_jwt_token=token.invalido.x" "$BASE_URL/accounts")" = "401" ] || fail "token inválido deveria ser 401"
ok "token inválido -> 401"

me=$(curl -s -H "$COOKIE" "$BASE_URL/auth/me")
echo "$me" | grep -q "$EMAIL" || fail "GET /auth/me: $me"
ok "GET /auth/me devolve a conta logada"

ID=$(echo "$me" | sed -n 's/.*"id":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p')
# RBAC (bottleneck de autorização): conta nova é USER
[ "$(status -H "$COOKIE" "$BASE_URL/accounts/$ID")" = "200" ] || fail "GET /accounts/{próprio id}"
ok "GET /accounts/{próprio id} -> 200"
[ "$(status -H "$COOKIE" "$BASE_URL/accounts")" = "403" ] || fail "USER listou todas as contas"
ok "RBAC: USER em GET /accounts (listar todos) -> 403"
[ "$(status -H "$COOKIE" "$BASE_URL/accounts/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000")" = "403" ] || fail "USER viu conta de outro"
ok "RBAC: USER em GET /accounts/{outro id} -> 403"
[ "$(status -X DELETE -H "$COOKIE" "$BASE_URL/accounts/$ID")" = "403" ] || fail "USER apagou conta"
ok "RBAC: USER em DELETE /accounts/{id} -> 403"

[ "$(status "$BASE_URL/exchange/USD/BRL")" = "401" ] || fail "GET /exchange sem token deveria ser 401"
ok "GET /exchange/USD/BRL sem token -> 401"

# o exchange depende de uma API externa: 503 (fora do ar/limite) vira só aviso
ex=$(curl -s -w '\n%{http_code}' -H "$COOKIE" "$BASE_URL/exchange/USD/BRL")
code=$(echo "$ex" | tail -1); body=$(echo "$ex" | sed '$d')
case "$code" in
  200)
    echo "$body" | grep -q '"sell"' && echo "$body" | grep -q '"buy"' || fail "GET /exchange/USD/BRL: $body"
    echo "$body" | grep -q "\"id-account\":\"$ID\"" || fail "exchange não recebeu o id-account do gateway: $body"
    ok "GET /exchange/USD/BRL -> 200 com sell/buy e o id-account do usuário" ;;
  503) echo "aviso - exchange respondeu 503 (API de câmbio externa indisponível)" ;;
  *) fail "GET /exchange/USD/BRL respondeu $code: $body" ;;
esac
[ "$(status -H "$COOKIE" "$BASE_URL/exchanges/USD/XX")" = "400" ] || fail "/exchanges/{from}/{to} (apelido) deveria chegar no exchange"
ok "GET /exchanges/... (apelido) chega no exchange"

hosts=$(for i in $(seq 1 12); do curl -s "$BASE_URL/health-check"; echo; done | sort -u | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
if [ "$hosts" -ge 2 ]; then ok "balanceamento: $hosts réplicas diferentes do gateway responderam"
else echo "aviso - só 1 réplica do gateway respondeu (GATEWAY_REPLICAS=1?)"; fi

if command -v docker >/dev/null && docker compose ps redis >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  keys=$(docker compose exec -T redis redis-cli --scan --pattern 'gateway:token:*' | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
  [ "$keys" -ge 1 ] || fail "nenhum token em cache no redis"
  ok "cache: $keys token(s) em cache no Redis (chave = SHA-256 do JWT)"
fi

[ "$(status "$BASE_URL/gateway/actuator/prometheus")" = "404" ] || fail "métricas não deveriam ser públicas"
ok "/gateway/actuator/prometheus bloqueado no lb"

logout=$(curl -s -D - -o /dev/null "$BASE_URL/auth/logout")
echo "$logout" | grep -qi 'set-cookie: __store_jwt_token=;' || fail "logout não limpou o cookie"
ok "GET /auth/logout limpa o cookie"

echo ">> smoke test passou"

docs.title: On EKS
docs.text:
Deployment to EKS is done by the pipeline (CI/CD): each service applies its own k8s/ and the platform repository applies the shared infrastructure (k8s/lb.yaml and k8s/redis.yaml). To apply it manually:

aws eks update-kubeconfig --name <cluster> --region <região>

kubectl apply -n store -f k8s/                         # lb (Nginx + LoadBalancer) e redis
kubectl apply -n store -f api/gateway-service/k8s/     # gateway
kubectl get svc lb -n store                            # endereço público do ELB
BASE_URL=http://<endereço-do-elb> ./scripts/smoke-test.sh

docs.title: Use of AI
docs.text:
The assignment allows partial use of AI in the implementation, as long as it is documented: what was done with AI help, what was done by the group, and everyone must be able to explain and defend any part (including the AI-generated ones). This page is that record — each member fills in their own part.

Group rule

Nothing generated by AI goes in unless the owner has read, run and understood it. Before the presentation we do an internal walkthrough in which each member explains the others' parts.

docs.title: Leonardo
docs.text:
Tool: Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5 model, Anthropic), running in the terminal with access to the organization's GitHub.

How it was used: based on the project board and the course material (hands-on 2, 3, 4, 7 and 8 and the bottlenecks page), I asked the AI to implement my tasks. The AI generated the code, ran the tests and the platform locally, and opened the repositories/PRs. What I reviewed and changed is recorded below.

Part Done with AI? Notes Gateway (pna26/gateway-service) Yes — code generated by the AI from hands-on 3 Changes relative to the hands-on (filter order, 401/503, AuthClient with timeout) are justified in Gateway. 20 automated tests. Token cache in Redis Yes The choice to cache /auth/solve in the gateway and the TTL/key rules are in Cache. Tested with Redis on and off. Nginx (load balancing) Yes — from hands-on 7 Added resolve (scaling without reload) and blocking of the actuator. Reusable CI/CD pipeline Yes Trivy steps simulated locally before publishing. Vulnerability scanning Yes The Dockerfile and k8s manifest fixes came from Trivy's own findings. platform's compose.yaml, scripts and k8s manifests Yes Manifests validated with Trivy and nginx -t. On 12/11 they ran on a kind cluster matching eks-store (Gabriel's rehearsal, see Load testing); not yet on the real EKS. This documentation (structure and the text of my parts) Yes Based on the professor's template. Measurements (load balancing, cache) Run by the AI on my machine The numbers are the ones output by the commands shown on the pages. AWS in the pipeline via OIDC (service.yaml, infra.yaml, CI/CD) Yes — from Nicolas's proposal (role github-actions-pna26) Validated with actionlint. Reviewing it with the AI surfaced three points that were not in the plan: the merge order (the reusable workflow cannot request more permissions than its caller), the account, auth and notification-service repositories also needing id-token: write, and AmazonEKSEditPolicy not letting infra create Prometheus's Role/RoleBinding. Review of Nicolas's PRs (EKS and messaging) Yes — reading the diffs with the AI The decision to merge and the review comments are mine. Review of Gabriel's HPA test (#9) and adjustments (#10) Yes The AI built the docs, checked the new panel against the k8s Prometheus and found that kubectl autoscale --cpu=50% does not exist before kubectl 1.34 (mine was 1.33). The keepalive_time 10s in lb came from Gabriel's finding; validated with nginx -t on the manifest's image. HTTPS in Architecture, Home status and the Presentation script Yes Put together from the code (Auth cookie), the course assignment and the state of the repositories. Presentation video and 20/11 delivery (script, recording the pages with Playwright, editing with ffmpeg, scripts/eks-hpa.sh and scripts/fill-eks-hpa.py) and English translation (Home, bottlenecks) Yes The AI wrote the scripts and recorded the documentation scenes. The EKS demo only uses HTTP through the ELB, with the JWT and password hidden on screen. The EKS table only receives numbers from the k6 and HPA summary: anything not measured stays "—".

What I (Leonardo) did without AI:

  • Project organization: I created the project board (26/10/2026) with the 22 task cards: the split of work among the three members, the weight of each deliverable and the owner of each item.
  • Group scope: I defined what each member delivers (services, bottlenecks, parts of the infra and the documentation) and the shared tasks (local compose, internal walkthrough, presentation).
  • API contract: I wrote the "Contrato de API Gateway/Auth/Account" card, the basis of the Architecture page: Gateway, Auth, Account and Exchange routes, open routes, JWT claims and duration, cookie configuration and the open questions, each with an owner (login route in Account, /exchange × /exchanges, service names in compose/k8s, HTTPS on EKS).
  • Review of the code generated by the AI: gateway, CI/CD pipeline, compose.yaml, Nginx and k8s manifests.
  • Directing the work with the AI: I chose which tasks would be done and approved each external action: creation of the gateway-service and platform repositories, CI PRs on Nicolas's repositories (via fork, for him to review) and board updates.

Where the AI got it wrong and it was fixed:

  • The first with/without cache benchmark was invalid: the TOKEN_CACHE_ENABLED variable was not being passed by compose to the gateway, so both runs used the cache. It was fixed and measured again; the honest conclusion is that locally the latency stays the same and the gain is taking load off Auth.
  • Trivy aborts when --ignorefile points to a file that does not exist: the pipeline now only uses .trivyignore when it exists (the Account/Auth repositories don't have one).
  • WebClient.Builder is no longer auto-configured in Spring Boot 4 without spring-boot-starter-webclient (the integration test caught this).

docs.title: Nicolas
docs.text:
Tool: Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5 model, Anthropic), in the terminal and the desktop app, with access to the local clone of platform, the organization's GitHub and, for the AWS steps, the AWS CLI logged in via SSO.

How it was used: I used the AI to look up what should be done correctly and to structure the code. Before each task, it read the course material (Hands-on 1, 3 and 7 and the EKS and bottlenecks pages) and explained what the professor expects and the right way to do it. Then it built the structure (classes, migrations, manifests, commands) following the patterns of the course and the group's repositories. I reviewed what the AI did, understanding each step: I read each change, asked for an explanation of what was not clear and only moved on once I understood what had been done and why.

Part Done with AI? Notes Account (account + account-service) Yes — structure from Hands-on 1 Resource, Service, Parser, Model, Repository, Flyway and Dockerfile. The login route in Account (POST /accounts/login) came from Hands-on 3. All routes tested in compose. Auth (auth + auth-service) Yes — structure from Hands-on 3 JwtService (JJWT) and AuthService calling Account via Feign. Tested register, login, tampered token (401), me and logout. AWS Yes — explanation of each step; I ran the commands and did the console clicks myself Budget, region, SSO in the AWS CLI, ECR and the GitHub Actions OIDC role. The AI explained beforehand and checked the result afterwards. EKS Yes — manifests, setup/eks-store.yaml, RDS and the order for creating and deleting First manual deploy on 08/11. On 16/11 the AI brought the environment up with my authorization, the CI deploy worked for my three services and everything was deleted afterwards. Messaging (Kafka) Yes — code, compose, k8s manifests, test script and the page Adapted from Hands-on 7 (transactional outbox, idempotent consumer, DLT), swapping orders for accounts. scripts/messaging-test.sh passing in compose; on EKS, the event reached notification-service on 16/11. notification-service (new repository) Yes Spring Kafka consumer following the pattern of Hands-on 7 and the group's repositories (Dockerfile, CI, k8s). Authorization (RBAC) Yes — the AI found the flaw by reading the gateway and account, and structured the solution Any logged-in user could list, view and delete other people's accounts. USER/ADMIN role in Account, role claim in the JWT and rules in the gateway. Tested in compose with two accounts and in CI (13 new tests). The change to Leonardo's gateway went through a PR.

What I (Nicolas) did without AI:

  • AWS by hand: I ran the commands and did the console clicks (budget, SSO, ECR, CI role), checking each result with the AI.
  • Project decisions: region us-east-2 and a US$ 20/month cost alert; RDS PostgreSQL for the database on EKS; nodes only in private subnets and RDS without public access; deleting the environment whenever it is not in use; in messaging, the welcome email as the use case, the consumer in a separate service and following the professor's material (Kafka) instead of the RabbitMQ in the initial plan; in RBAC, new accounts are always USER and ADMIN only via the database.
  • Review: I read and understood each change before it went to GitHub, and tested in compose and on the cluster.
  • Rules for the AI: no secrets in Git, on screen or in logs; commits without AI co-authorship; changes to another member's repository only through PRs, for the owner to review. I approved each external action.

Where the AI got it wrong and it was fixed:

  • OIDC rejected in the first CI run (Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity): the trust policy expected repo:pna26/*, but the repositories use GitHub's immutable subject (repo:pna26@<id>/...). Fixed and documented in AWS.
  • ECR names: the first repositories (gateway, auth...) did not match the names the pipeline uses (*-service). They were recreated with the right names and the old, empty ones deleted.
  • docker login to ECR failed on Windows: the token exceeds the size the Credential Manager accepts. Solved with docker-credential-ecr-login.
  • CI permissions on the cluster: AmazonEKSEditPolicy did not allow creating Prometheus's Role, and not even AmazonEKSAdminPolicy solved it, because Kubernetes' privilege-escalation check does not see the AWS policy. The fix was a RoleBinding to the admin role, only in the store namespace.
  • Fallback JWT key in Auth's application.yaml: removed during the security review, and now Auth does not start without JWT_SECRET_KEY.
  • It used saveAndFlush, which does not exist in account's CrudRepository: the build caught it and it became save (the transaction still guarantees that the account and the event are saved together).
  • The messaging script failed in Git Bash on Windows: /opt/kafka/... became C:/Program Files/Git/opt/.... Fixed with MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1.
  • smoke-test.sh expected any user to be able to GET /accounts (200); with RBAC it became 403, and the script got the new checks. The first JwtService test did not compile (invalid escape in a regular expression), and the build caught it before the commit.

docs.title: Bottlenecks
docs.text:
Bottlenecks identified in the platform and what was done about each one (the assignment asks for at least 2 per member).

Bottleneck Problem Mitigation Owner Status Load balancing A single gateway is a single point of failure and of capacity Nginx in front of N gateway replicas (compose and EKS) Leonardo done Cache Every authenticated request called Auth (/auth/solve) Redis shared across the replicas: token → account id Leonardo done Vulnerability scanning Dependencies, images and manifests with known flaws Trivy (SCA, image, secrets, IaC) in the pipeline + OWASP ZAP (DAST) Leonardo done Exchange rate cache Every quote called the external API (third-party latency, rate limit) In-memory cache per pair: 30 s TTL, lock against stampede, stale-if-error Gabriel done Observability No visibility into behavior under load Prometheus (discovers every replica) + Grafana with a versioned dashboard, on compose and on EKS Gabriel done Messaging Welcome e-mail on the sign-up path: provider latency and outages become sign-up latency and outages Kafka: account publishes AccountCreated (transactional outbox) and notification-service consumes it idempotently, with retries and DLT Nicolas done (compose and EKS, with deploy from CI on 16/11) Authorization (RBAC) Any logged-in user could list, view and delete other people's accounts Role (USER/ADMIN) in Account, role claim in the JWT and rules in the gateway: USER only sees their own account (403 for the rest) Nicolas done (compose)

docs.title: Cache (Redis)
docs.text: Owner: Leonardo

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Without a cache, every authenticated request makes the gateway call Auth (POST /auth/solve) before moving on to the target service. Auth becomes a bottleneck and a point of failure on the path of every route, even when the same user repeats the same token hundreds of times.

And since the gateway has several replicas behind Nginx, an in-memory cache in each JVM would not solve it: replica 2 would not see what replica 1 already validated.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Cache-aside pattern with a Redis shared by all gateway replicas:

flowchart LR
    gw["gateway<br/>(any replica)"] -->|"1. GET gateway:token:<sha256>"| redis[(Redis)]
    redis -->|"2a. hit → account id"| gw
    redis -->|"2b. miss"| gw
    gw -->|"3. POST /auth/solve (only on miss)"| auth[Auth]
    auth -->|"4. idAccount"| gw
    gw -->|"5. SET ... EX min(5 min, exp)"| redis
Decision Reason Key = gateway:token: + SHA-256 of the JWT Redis never stores the token itself; whoever reads Redis cannot reuse tokens. TTL = the lower of 5 min and the JWT exp An expired token never stays valid because of the cache. Only stores valid tokens An invalid token does not go into the cache: it keeps being rejected by Auth (401). Redis down → carries on without cache The cache is an optimization: if it goes down, the gateway goes back to calling Auth (validation is still mandatory). The Redis health check was turned off in the actuator so the gateway does not show "DOWN" because of it. Metric gateway_token_cache_total{result=hit\|miss\|error} Shows in Prometheus/Grafana how many validations the cache saved. TOKEN_CACHE_ENABLED=false Allows comparing with and without cache in the load test.

Known limitation

The JWT is stateless: after logout the cookie is deleted in the browser, but the token stays valid until exp (with or without cache). The cache does not make this worse, because the TTL never goes past exp.

docs.title: Code
Results
docs.text:
Measured locally (Docker Desktop, Mac M-series), with ab -n 3000 -c 20 on a protected route and 2 gateway replicas:

Metric Value Authenticated requests 3001 Resolved by Redis (hit) 3000 Calls to Auth (miss) 1

In other words, Auth was taken off the path of 99.97% of requests. With Redis stopped (docker compose stop redis) the gateway kept responding 200 with a valid token and 401 without a token, only logging redis indisponível, seguindo sem cache.

Latency

On the local machine, latency with and without cache was within the noise (≈ 700–1600 req/s in both configurations), because all containers share the same CPU and /auth/solve is just an HMAC check: going to Redis costs almost the same as going to Auth. The gain here is taking load off Auth (and off Account, when Auth needs to query it). The latency effect should be measured on EKS, in the load test, comparing TOKEN_CACHE_ENABLED=true and false.

To check the cache:

docker compose exec redis redis-cli --scan --pattern 'gateway:token:*'
docker compose exec redis redis-cli TTL gateway:token:<hash>

docs.title: Exchange rate cache (Exchange)
docs.text:
Owner: Gabriel

Provider

The measurements on this page were taken with AwesomeAPI. Since 20/11 the default provider is the Central Bank of Brazil's PTAX (Exchange); the cache (30 s TTL, per-pair lock and stale-if-error) is the same and still needed: PTAX is a public service, never load-test it.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Exchange depends on a third-party API (AwesomeAPI). Without a cache, every GET /exchange/USD/BRL request turns into an HTTP call outside our network:

  • the latency of a service we do not control (tens to hundreds of ms, sometimes seconds) lands on the path of every request;
  • the free API has a rate limit: under load it starts responding 429, and then Exchange goes down for all users, not just for whoever generated the load;
  • if the external API goes down, Exchange goes down with it.

It is the same pattern as the token cache in the gateway, but here the bottleneck is outside the platform.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
In-memory cache inside Exchange itself, per currency pair:

flowchart LR
    r["N requests<br/>USD → BRL"] --> ex[exchange]
    ex -->|"quote < 30 s old?"| hit{hit}
    hit -->|yes| resp([response])
    hit -->|no| lock["pair lock<br/>(only 1 fetch)"]
    lock -->|"1 call"| api([AwesomeAPI])
    api -->|ok| save["store in cache"] --> resp
    api -->|"failure / 429"| stale{"quote<br/>< 10 min old?"}
    stale -->|yes| resp
    stale -->|no| e503([503])
Decision Reason 30 s TTL (CACHE_TTL) A 30-second-old quote is acceptable for a store; this way each replica makes at most 2 calls/min per pair, regardless of load. Process memory, not Redis There are few pairs (tiny cardinality) and the data is public: losing the cache on a restart costs 1 call. A shared Redis would only save replicas − 1 calls every 30 s. One lock per pair When the cache expires with 200 users asking for USD-BRL at the same time, only one request calls the API and the others wait and read the cache (avoids cache stampede). Stale-if-error for up to 10 min (CACHE_STALE_TTL) If the external API fails or returns 429, we serve the last known quote instead of 503. Nonexistent pair (404) does not go into the cache Client errors are not cached. 3 s timeout on the external call A slow API does not hold Exchange's connections indefinitely. CACHE_TTL=0 turns it off For comparison in the load test.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
app/cache.py
"""Bottleneck: cache da cotação.

Sem cache, cada GET /exchange/USD/BRL vira uma chamada HTTP para a API externa:
latência de rede de terceiros no caminho de toda requisição e risco de bater no
limite de requisições da API (que derruba o serviço para todo mundo).

Decisões:
  - cache em memória por par, TTL curto (CACHE_TTL, padrão 30 s): cotação de
    30 s atrás é aceitável para uma loja, e a cardinalidade é minúscula
    (poucos pares de moedas), então não precisa de Redis;
  - um lock por par: com 200 usuários pedindo USD-BRL no mesmo instante em que
    o cache expira, só UMA chamada vai para a API externa (evita "cache stampede");
  - se a API externa falhar, devolve a última cotação conhecida por até
    CACHE_STALE_TTL (padrão 10 min) em vez de 503 ("stale-if-error").
"""

import asyncio
import time
from typing import Awaitable, Callable

from prometheus_client import Counter

from .provider import PairNotFound, Quote, UpstreamError

CACHE_RESULTS = Counter(
    "exchange_quote_cache",
    "Resultado da consulta ao cache de cotações",
    ["result"],  # hit | miss | stale | error
)

Fetcher = Callable[[str, str], Awaitable[Quote]]


class QuoteCache:
    def __init__(self, fetch: Fetcher, ttl: float, stale_ttl: float, clock: Callable[[], float] = time.monotonic):
        self._fetch = fetch
        self._ttl = ttl
        self._stale_ttl = stale_ttl
        self._clock = clock
        self._entries: dict[tuple[str, str], tuple[Quote, float]] = {}
        self._locks: dict[tuple[str, str], asyncio.Lock] = {}

    def _fresh(self, key: tuple[str, str]) -> Quote | None:
        entry = self._entries.get(key)
        if entry and self._clock() - entry[1] < self._ttl:
            return entry[0]
        return None

    async def get(self, src: str, dst: str) -> Quote:
        key = (src, dst)
        if self._ttl > 0 and (quote := self._fresh(key)):
            CACHE_RESULTS.labels("hit").inc()
            return quote

        lock = self._locks.setdefault(key, asyncio.Lock())
        async with lock:
            # outra requisição pode ter atualizado o cache enquanto esperávamos o lock
            if self._ttl > 0 and (quote := self._fresh(key)):
                CACHE_RESULTS.labels("hit").inc()
                return quote

            try:
                quote = await self._fetch(src, dst)
            except PairNotFound:
                CACHE_RESULTS.labels("miss").inc()
                raise
            except UpstreamError:
                entry = self._entries.get(key)
                if entry and self._clock() - entry[1] < self._stale_ttl:
                    CACHE_RESULTS.labels("stale").inc()
                    return entry[0]
                CACHE_RESULTS.labels("error").inc()
                raise

            CACHE_RESULTS.labels("miss").inc()
            self._entries[key] = (quote, self._clock())
            return quote

docs.title: How to verify
docs.text:
The service's tests prove the behavior without depending on the real API (tests/test_cache.py):

Test Expected result 50 consecutive requests to /exchange/USD/BRL 1 call to the external API 100 concurrent requests with an empty cache 1 call to the external API API down 2 min after the last quote 200 with the previous quote (stale) API down 11 min later 503

With the platform running, the metric exchange_quote_cache_total{result="hit|miss|stale|error"} shows the hit rate in Grafana (Observability).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Measured on 05/11/2026 by the load test (experiment 3: 10 users, 30 s, GET /exchange/USD/BRL and EUR/BRL through lb → gateway → exchange, against the real AwesomeAPI):

EXCHANGE_CACHE_TTL Requests p50 p95 p99 Errors 0 (no cache) 445 23 ms 49 ms 69 ms 0 % 30 (with cache) 454 3 ms 4 ms 17 ms 0 %

p95 drops by 92%: without cache, the latency of every quote is that of the external API; with cache, only the first quote of each pair every 30 s pays that latency. The biggest gain does not show in the table: without cache, the external API received ≈ 7 calls per second from just 10 users; with cache, it receives at most 2 per minute per pair and per replica, regardless of load — far from the free API's rate limit.

Earlier, running the service on its own against the real API: the first USD/BRL lookup took 60 ms (external call), the next one 1.5 ms (cache).

docs.title: Load balancing
docs.text: Owner: Leonardo

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: With a single gateway, the whole platform depends on one process: if it goes down, nothing responds; if it saturates, there is no way to scale. Since the gateway is the only entry point, it is the first bottleneck.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
An Nginx (lb) becomes the only exposed service and distributes requests across several gateway replicas (Round Robin, the default of the upstream block). The gateway no longer publishes a port.

Docker ComposeEKS 
flowchart LR
    user([User]) e0@==>|":8080"| lb["lb · Nginx :80"]:::orange
    subgraph trusted [compose internal network]
        lb e1@==> g1[gateway-1]
        lb e2@==> g2[gateway-2]
        lb e3@==> g3[gateway-N]
    end
    e0@{ animate: true }
    e1@{ animate: true }
    e2@{ animate: true }
    e3@{ animate: true }
    classDef orange fill:#FCBE3E
flowchart LR
    user([User]) e0@==> elb["AWS ELB<br/>(Service lb, LoadBalancer)"]
    subgraph eks [EKS cluster]
        elb --> n1["lb pod 1 · Nginx"]:::orange
        elb --> n2["lb pod 2 · Nginx"]:::orange
        n1 & n2 --> svc["Service gateway<br/>(ClusterIP)"]
        svc --> g1[gateway pod 1]
        svc --> g2[gateway pod 2]
    end
    e0@{ animate: true }
    classDef orange fill:#FCBE3E

On EKS there are two levels: the AWS ELB spreads traffic across the Nginx pods (which also have 2 replicas, so the load balancer itself is not a single point of failure) and the gateway Service spreads it across the gateway pods.

$ for i in $(seq 1 15); do curl -s localhost:8080/health-check; echo; done | sort | uniq -c

docs.title: k8s manifest
Messaging (Kafka)
docs.text:
Owner: Nicolas

Follows the course's Hands-on 7 — Mensageria assíncrona (Kafka in compose, transactional outbox, idempotent consumer and DLT), adapted from BoxOffice's ticket sales to the store's account sign-up.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
After creating an account, the store wants to send a welcome email. If account called the email service inside POST /accounts, sign-up would be coupled to it:

  • the user would wait for the email provider's latency (tens to hundreds of ms per send);
  • an email outage would become a sign-up outage;
  • a spike in sign-ups would hit the email provider at the same moment, at the same pace.

Work the user does not need to wait for leaves the request path and goes to a broker.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    u([User]) -->|"POST /auth/register"| auth --> account
    subgraph tx ["one PostgreSQL transaction"]
        account -->|"INSERT"| acc[("accounts.accounts")]
        account -->|"INSERT AccountCreated"| ob[("accounts.outbox")]
    end
    relay["OutboxRelay<br/>(every 200 ms)"] -->|"reads pending"| ob
    relay -->|"key = account id<br/>acks=all"| k[["Kafka<br/>account-events (6 partitions)"]]
    k -->|"notification group"| n["notification-service"]
    n -->|"dedupe by eventId"| pe[("notification.processed_events")]
    n -->|SMTP| mail(["Mailpit"])
    n -. "permanent failure" .-> dlt[["account-events-dlt"]]
    dlt --> dl[("notification.dead_letters")]

The user's request ends at the database commit. Publishing, sending the email and retrying happen afterwards, asynchronously, and can be slow, fail or repeat without the user noticing.

Decision Reason Kafka (4.3, a single node in KRaft mode) It is the broker from the course material (Hands-on 7). The log is retained after consumption: messages can be reprocessed and a new consumer can read the history. Transactional outbox in account Saving the account and then publishing to Kafka are two writes to different systems: if the process dies between them, the event is lost (or an event is published for an account that does not exist). With the outbox, the account and the event go into the same transaction; a relay publishes after the commit. A duplicate email (rollback) leaves no orphan event. Relay with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED Several account replicas can run the relay without publishing the same row twice at the same time. Producer with acks=all and enable.idempotence The broker only acknowledges after writing; a producer resend does not duplicate the message in the log. Message key = account id Events for the same account land in the same partition: Kafka only guarantees ordering within a partition. 6 partitions, created by kafka-init The number of partitions is the cap on the group's parallel consumers. Auto-creation is turned off (it would give 1 partition). Idempotent consumer Delivery is at-least-once: the same event can arrive twice (the consumer died after sending and before committing the offset, or reprocessing). The eventId is saved in processed_events in the same transaction as the email record; if it already exists, the event is ignored. 3 retries with backoff (0.5 s, 1 s, 2 s) and DLT A temporary failure (SMTP down) is retried; after that the message goes to account-events-dlt and the partition keeps moving. Invalid JSON or an event missing required fields goes straight to the DLT: retrying would not help. The event carries no password or hash Only eventId, eventType, accountId, name, email and occurredAt: the minimum for the email. Its own schema (notification) The consumer keeps its state in the same PostgreSQL, without touching account's tables. Kafka with no published port; Kafka UI and Mailpit only on 127.0.0.1 The broker has no authentication: it stays in the trusted layer (compose network / ClusterIP on k8s), like Redis.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
AccountService saves the account and the event in the same transaction:

AccountService.java (excerpt)
    // conta e evento AccountCreated na mesma transação (transactional outbox):
    // ou os dois são gravados, ou nenhum (ex.: e-mail duplicado desfaz tudo)
    @Transactional
    public Account create(Account account) {

        if (null == account.password()) {
            throw new ResponseStatusException(
                HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "Password is empty"
            );
        }

        final String pass = account.password().trim();
        if (pass.length() < 6) {
            throw new ResponseStatusException(
                HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "Password must have at least 6 characters"
            );
        }

        if (account.email() == null || account.email().trim().isEmpty()) {
            throw new ResponseStatusException(
                HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "Email is empty"
            );
        }

        account.hashPassword(calcHash(pass));
        // RBAC: toda conta nova é USER; o papel nunca vem da requisição
        account.role(Role.USER.name());

        final Account saved = accountRepository.save(
            new AccountModel(account)
        ).to();

        final AccountEvent event = AccountEvent.created(saved);
        outbox.append(event.eventId(), "account", saved.id(), event.eventType(), event);
OutboxRelay.java
package store.account.outbox;

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.UUID;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.JdbcTemplate;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient;
import org.springframework.kafka.core.KafkaTemplate;
import org.springframework.kafka.support.SendResult;
import org.springframework.scheduling.annotation.Scheduled;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

/** Publica no Kafka os eventos que o Outbox gravou, depois do commit (Hands-on 7). */
@Component
public class OutboxRelay {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(OutboxRelay.class);

    record Pending(UUID id, String aggregateId, String eventType, String payload) {
    }

    private final JdbcClient jdbc;
    private final JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate;
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka;
    private final String topic;

    public OutboxRelay(JdbcClient jdbc, JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate,
                       KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka,
                       @Value("${store.account.topic}") String topic) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
        this.jdbcTemplate = jdbcTemplate;
        this.kafka = kafka;
        this.topic = topic;
    }

    @Scheduled(fixedDelayString = "${store.account.relay-interval-ms:200}")
    @Transactional
    public void relay() throws Exception {
        // SKIP LOCKED: várias réplicas do account podem rodar o relay sem pegar as mesmas linhas
        List<Pending> batch = jdbc.sql("""
                SELECT id, aggregate_id, event_type, payload::text AS payload
                FROM accounts.outbox
                WHERE published_at IS NULL
                ORDER BY created_at
                LIMIT 100
                FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
                """)
                .query(Pending.class)
                .list();
        if (batch.isEmpty()) {
            return;
        }

        List<CompletableFuture<SendResult<String, String>>> acks = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Pending p : batch) {
            // chave = id da conta: eventos da mesma conta caem na mesma partição (ordem por chave)
            ProducerRecord<String, String> record =
                    new ProducerRecord<>(topic, p.aggregateId(), p.payload());
            record.headers().add("eventId", p.id().toString().getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            record.headers().add("eventType", p.eventType().getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            acks.add(kafka.send(record));
        }
        // espera o ack de todos; se falhar, a transação volta e as linhas são tentadas de novo
        CompletableFuture.allOf(acks.toArray(new CompletableFuture<?>[0])).get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

        jdbcTemplate.batchUpdate("UPDATE accounts.outbox SET published_at = clock_timestamp() WHERE id = ?",
                batch.stream().map(p -> new Object[] {p.id()}).toList());
        log.info("relayed {} event(s) to {}", batch.size(), topic);
    }

    @Scheduled(cron = "0 0 * * * *")
    @Transactional
    public void purge() {
        int n = jdbcTemplate.update(
                "DELETE FROM accounts.outbox WHERE published_at < now() - interval '1 day'");
        log.info("purged {} published outbox row(s)", n);
    }
}

notification-service deduplicates by eventId before sending:

NotificationService.java
package store.notification;

import java.time.OffsetDateTime;
import java.time.ZoneOffset;

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Service
public class NotificationService {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(NotificationService.class);

    private final JdbcClient jdbc;
    private final EmailSender email;
    private final NotificationProperties props;

    public NotificationService(JdbcClient jdbc, EmailSender email, NotificationProperties props) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
        this.email = email;
        this.props = props;
    }

    /**
     * Entrega at-least-once: o mesmo evento pode chegar duas vezes. O eventId é
     * gravado na mesma transação do registro do e-mail; se já existir, é duplicata.
     *
     * @return true se enviou o e-mail, false se o evento era duplicado
     */
    @Transactional
    public boolean handle(AccountEvent e) {
        if (props.idempotent()) {
            int fresh = jdbc.sql("INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id) VALUES (?) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING")
                    .param(e.eventId())
                    .update();
            if (fresh == 0) {
                log.info("duplicate event {} for account {} ignored", e.eventId(), e.accountId());
                return false;
            }
        }
        email.welcome(e); // se lançar, a transação inteira volta (inclusive a linha de deduplicação)
        jdbc.sql("""
                INSERT INTO notifications (event_id, account_id, email, kind, occurred_at)
                VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
                """)
                .params(e.eventId(), e.accountId(), e.email(), e.eventType(),
                        OffsetDateTime.ofInstant(e.occurredAt(), ZoneOffset.UTC))
                .update();
        log.info("welcome e-mail sent for account {}", e.accountId());
        return true;
    }
}
KafkaConfig.java (retries and DLT)
package store.notification;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.kafka.core.KafkaTemplate;
import org.springframework.kafka.listener.DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer;
import org.springframework.kafka.listener.DefaultErrorHandler;
import org.springframework.kafka.support.ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries;

import tools.jackson.core.JacksonException;

@Configuration
public class KafkaConfig {

    /** Usado pela fábrica de listeners do Spring Boot (um único bean CommonErrorHandler). */
    @Bean
    DefaultErrorHandler errorHandler(KafkaTemplate<String, String> template) {
        // depois das tentativas, publica em <tópico>-dlt, mesma partição, com a exceção nos headers
        DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer recoverer = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template);

        ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries backOff = new ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries(3);
        backOff.setInitialInterval(500L);  // 0,5 s, 1 s, 2 s
        backOff.setMultiplier(2.0);
        backOff.setMaxInterval(5_000L);

        DefaultErrorHandler handler = new DefaultErrorHandler(recoverer, backOff);
        // falhas permanentes: tentar de novo não adianta, vai direto para a DLT
        handler.addNotRetryableExceptions(JacksonException.class, IllegalArgumentException.class);
        return handler;
    }
}

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
scripts/messaging-test.sh on local compose (08/11/2026), 20 sign-ups per experiment, simulated email latency of 50 ms, 3 consumer threads:

Experiment What happened 1. Happy path 20 sign-ups, average of 16 ms per POST /auth/register; 20 welcome emails in Mailpit. 2. notification stopped Sign-up kept responding (15 ms). The group lag rose to 20 messages, held in Kafka. When it came back, the backlog drained in 9 s (including JVM startup) and the 20 emails arrived. 3. Kafka stopped Sign-up kept responding (15 ms): the 20 events stayed in the outbox. With Kafka back, the relay published everything and the 20 emails arrived, no event lost. 4. Reprocessing (group offsets reset to the beginning) The whole topic was reread and no new email was sent: every event was already in processed_events. 5. Poison message (text that is not JSON) Went to account-events-dlt without retry (StreamReadException) and stayed in dead_letters. The next 20 sign-ups produced the 20 emails: the partition did not get stuck.

Also checked: a second sign-up with the same email (500, the course's behavior) does not leave a row in the outbox, because the rollback undoes the account and the event together.

With the email in the synchronous path

With the send inside the request, each sign-up would add the provider's latency (50 ms simulated here, and hundreds of ms with real providers) and would fail along with it. In experiments 2 and 3 sign-up took the same time with the consumer or the broker down: that is the decoupling the bottleneck calls for.

docs.title: On EKS
docs.text:
Ran on eks-store on 16/11/2026, deployed by CI (evidence):

  • k8s/kafka.yaml: 1-replica Deployment (KRaft), kafka Service (ClusterIP) and the kafka-init Job that creates the topics. The infra.yaml workflow applies the k8s/ folder along with the other manifests.
  • k8s/mailpit.yaml: fake SMTP; the inbox is reachable only via kubectl port-forward -n store svc/mailpit 8025:8025.
  • api/notification-service/k8s/k8s.yaml: the consumer (no Service: nobody calls it), published by the notification-service pipeline (run). account's ConfigMap gained KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS.
  • notification-secrets Secret (RDS user and password) created by hand, once per cluster, like account-secrets. It never goes to Git.

Result (16/11): a sign-up through Auth's kubectl port-forward (the gateway had not been published yet that day) returned 200; Flyway created the schema in RDS, the relay published the AccountCreated from the outbox to the account-events topic and notification-service logged the welcome email send (see EKS). The containers run with the same restrictions tested locally (non-root user, capabilities dropped, read-only root on Mailpit and on notification). The failure experiments (2 to 5 above) were done on compose.

Known limitations

  • Kafka without a persistent disk on EKS: the cluster does not have the EBS CSI driver, so the data lives in an emptyDir. If the Kafka pod restarts, messages not yet consumed are lost. In production: a PersistentVolume, 3 brokers with replication-factor 3, or Amazon MSK (managed Kafka).
  • A single broker (replication-factor 1): no tolerance to broker failure. Events wait in the outbox while it is down (experiment 3), but the broker is a single point of failure for messaging.
  • No authentication on Kafka (PLAINTEXT): acceptable only because it is not reachable from outside the internal network.
  • Consumer lag is not in Prometheus/Grafana yet; today it is seen through Kafka UI or the CLI.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: Owner: Gabriel

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: With several gateway replicas behind Nginx, a cache in Redis and a service that depends on an external API, there was no way to know what was happening under load: which replica gets more requests, whether the cache is hitting, whether errors come from the gateway or from Exchange, whether the JVM is close to its memory limit. Without that, the load test would only show the client's final number, without explaining why.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Prometheus scrapes each replica's metrics every 5 s and Grafana shows a dashboard versioned in the repository, provisioned automatically (no clicking through the UI).

flowchart LR
    subgraph trusted [Internal network]
        gw1["gateway 1"] & gw2["gateway 2"] -.->|"/gateway/actuator/prometheus"| prom[(Prometheus)]
        ex["exchange"] -.->|"/metrics"| prom
        prom --> graf[Grafana]
    end
    k6([k6]) -->|remote write| prom
    dev([you]) -->|"127.0.0.1:3000"| graf
Decision Reason dns_sd_configs in compose The name gateway resolves to all replica IPs; each one becomes a target (instance). With static_configs each scrape would land on a random replica and the series would get mixed up. --scale gateway=N is picked up on its own within 10 s. kubernetes_sd_configs + prometheus.io/* annotations on EKS Prometheus discovers the namespace's pods; anything that wants to be scraped just annotates the pod (gateway and exchange already do). RBAC with a read-only Role in the namespace, not a ClusterRole. Metrics off the internet lb answers 404 for /gateway/actuator/** and the gateway only forwards /exchange/** (exchange's /metrics is left out). Prometheus and Grafana: 127.0.0.1 in compose and ClusterIP + port-forward on EKS. Dashboard as JSON in git (setup/grafana/dashboards/store.json) The same file serves compose (volume) and EKS (ConfigMap created by the infra workflow). Dashboard changed → PR. k6 remote write The load test shows up on the same dashboard, on the same time axis as the server metrics. Grafana password out of git Compose: GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD in .env. EKS: Secret created by the workflow (org secret or random). Exchange with a histogram; gateway with mean/max Exchange publishes buckets (exchange_http_server_requests_seconds_bucket), so it has p50/p95/p99. Spring Boot does not publish buckets by default; the client-side percentiles come from k6.

docs.title: Metrics used
docs.text:
Source Metric What for gateway (Micrometer) http_server_requests_seconds_{count,sum,max} req/s by status and by replica, mean/max latency, 5xx rate gateway gateway_token_cache_total{result} token cache hit rate gateway jvm_memory_used_bytes, process_cpu_usage memory and CPU per replica exchange exchange_http_server_requests_seconds (histogram, label route = template) quote req/s and p50/p95/p99 exchange exchange_quote_cache_total{result} quote cache hit rate exchange exchange_upstream_request_seconds{outcome} calls to and latency of the external API Prometheus up{job} replicas up (the HPA number and curve) k6 k6_vus, k6_http_reqs_total, k6_http_req_duration_p95/p99 applied load and latency seen by the client

Exchange's route label uses the route template (/exchange/{from_}/{to}), not the actual URL: otherwise each currency pair would create a new series in Prometheus (cardinality explosion). There is a test for this.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
Store — plataforma (Store folder, also Grafana's home page):

Row Panels Overview req/s, % of 5xx (green/orange/red), replicas up per service, token cache hit % Gateway replicas up over time (shows the HPA), req/s by status, mean/max latency, req/s per replica (shows the balancing), cache hit/miss/error, heap and CPU per replica Exchange quotes/s by status, p50/p95/p99, quote cache × calls to the external API Load test (k6) VUs and req/s, client p95/p99 per scenario

docs.text:
ComposeEKS 
docker compose up -d --build
# Grafana:    http://localhost:3000   (admin / GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD do .env)
# Prometheus: http://localhost:9090/targets   (uma linha por réplica)

kubectl get secret grafana-admin -n store -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d
