docs.title: Result: what observability showed
docs.text:
Verified on 05/11/2026 with the local platform up: Prometheus discovered the 2 gateway replicas and exchange on its own (/targets, all up), Grafana came up with the data source and the dashboard already provisioned, and every dashboard query returns data.

During the load test it was observability that explained the numbers k6 only showed from the outside:

Question Where the answer showed up Is the token cache really sparing Auth? gateway_token_cache_total: 7,571 hits × 21 misses in the run with cache (99.7 %). Why did 4 replicas deliver less than 1 at saturation? Machine CPU (system_cpu_usage) at ≈ 83–85 % in both runs: the replicas were competing for the same cores. Where did the 0.57 % errors at saturation come from? http_server_requests_seconds_count{status="500"} on the gateway (≈ 3,500) → Auth logs: BindException when calling Account (Feign without a connection pool). Do the replicas the HPA created get load right away? No: in the HPA test, "Requisições/s por réplica" showed the 4 new ones starting at 0 req/s and the load split evenly only ≈ 1.5 min after they became ready. lb reuses connections and the Kubernetes Service balances connections, not requests (finding). Fixed in lb with keepalive_time 10s (≈ 35–40 s in the trial run).

docs.title: During the HPA test
docs.text:
Grafana on EKS during the HPA test of 19/11 (result), from the start of the load to the end of k6: the gateway scales from 2 to 4 and then 6 replicas, with 0 % 5xx errors and the token cache hitting 100 %. The exchange row has no traffic because the auth scenario does not call the exchange service.

The same test, rehearsed earlier on a kind cluster (local trial run), showed the same pattern: 2 → 6 replicas in ≈ 1 min, 0 % errors.

For this test the dashboard gained the Réplicas no ar ao longo do tempo (HPA) panel (sum by (job) (up{job=~"gateway|exchange"}), as steps), and the "Erros 5xx" panel now shows 0 % instead of No data when there are no errors (... or vector(0) in the numerator).

Suggestion for the gateway (Leonardo)

Turning on spring.cloud.gateway.server.webflux.metrics.enabled=true in the gateway would publish spring_cloud_gateway_requests_seconds with the routeId, which would allow breaking latency down by route (auth × account × exchange). Also, management.metrics.distribution.percentiles-histogram.http.server.requests=true would give server-side p95/p99.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
setup/prometheus.ymlk8s/prometheus.yamlk8s/grafana.yaml 
# Bottleneck: observabilidade. Prometheus do compose local.
#
# O gateway e o exchange têm várias réplicas atrás do mesmo nome DNS. Com
# static_configs ("gateway:8080") cada scrape cairia numa réplica aleatória e as
# séries se misturariam; com dns_sd_configs o Prometheus resolve o nome para
# TODOS os IPs e raspa cada réplica separada (label "instance" = IP da réplica).
# "--scale gateway=N" entra sozinho em até 10 s.

global:
  scrape_interval: 5s
  evaluation_interval: 15s

scrape_configs:

  - job_name: gateway
    metrics_path: /gateway/actuator/prometheus
    dns_sd_configs:
      - names: [ gateway ]
        type: A
        port: 8080
        refresh_interval: 10s

  - job_name: exchange
    metrics_path: /metrics
    dns_sd_configs:
      - names: [ exchange ]
        type: A
        port: 8080
        refresh_interval: 10s

  - job_name: prometheus
    static_configs:
      - targets: [ localhost:9090 ]

# Bottleneck: observabilidade no EKS. O Prometheus descobre os pods do próprio
# namespace pela API do Kubernetes e raspa os que têm as anotações
#   prometheus.io/scrape: "true", prometheus.io/path, prometheus.io/port
# (gateway-service/k8s e exchange-service/k8s já trazem). Cada réplica vira um
# alvo separado. Acesso: kubectl port-forward svc/prometheus 9090 -n store
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: prometheus
---
# só leitura de pods/endpoints do namespace (Role, não ClusterRole)
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: prometheus
rules:
  - apiGroups: [ "" ]
    resources: [ pods, services, endpoints ]
    verbs: [ get, list, watch ]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: prometheus
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: prometheus
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: prometheus
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: prometheus-configmap
data:
  prometheus.yml: |
    global:
      scrape_interval: 15s
    scrape_configs:
      - job_name: pods
        kubernetes_sd_configs:
          - role: pod
            namespaces:
              own_namespace: true
        relabel_configs:
          - source_labels: [ __meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_scrape ]
            action: keep
            regex: "true"
          - source_labels: [ __meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_path ]
            action: replace
            target_label: __metrics_path__
            regex: (.+)
          - source_labels: [ __address__, __meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_port ]
            action: replace
            regex: ([^:]+)(?::\d+)?;(\d+)
            replacement: $1:$2
            target_label: __address__
          # job = label "app" do pod (gateway, exchange...), como no compose
          - source_labels: [ __meta_kubernetes_pod_label_app ]
            target_label: job
          - source_labels: [ __meta_kubernetes_pod_name ]
            target_label: pod
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: prometheus
  labels:
    app: prometheus
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: prometheus
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: prometheus
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: prometheus
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 65534
        runAsGroup: 65534
        fsGroup: 65534
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
      containers:
        - name: prometheus
          image: prom/prometheus:v3.5.0
          args:
            - --config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
            - --storage.tsdb.path=/prometheus
            # sem volume persistente: guarda só o suficiente para os testes/demonstração
            - --storage.tsdb.retention.time=2d
            - --web.enable-remote-write-receiver
          ports:
            - containerPort: 9090
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /-/ready
              port: 9090
            periodSeconds: 10
          resources:
            requests:
              memory: "256Mi"
              cpu: "100m"
            limits:
              memory: "512Mi"
              cpu: "500m"
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities:
              drop: [ "ALL" ]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /etc/prometheus
            - name: data
              mountPath: /prometheus
      volumes:
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: prometheus-configmap
        - name: data
          emptyDir: {}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: prometheus
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: prometheus
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 9090
      targetPort: 9090

# Bottleneck: observabilidade no EKS. Grafana sem porta pública (ClusterIP):
#   kubectl port-forward svc/grafana 3000 -n store   ->  http://localhost:3000
# O ConfigMap "grafana-dashboards" (setup/grafana/dashboards/*.json) e o Secret
# "grafana-admin" são criados pelo workflow infra (assim o JSON do dashboard
# não fica duplicado e a senha não fica no git).
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: grafana-provisioning
data:
  datasources.yaml: |
    apiVersion: 1
    datasources:
      - name: Prometheus
        uid: prometheus
        type: prometheus
        access: proxy
        url: http://prometheus:9090
        isDefault: true
  dashboards.yaml: |
    apiVersion: 1
    providers:
      - name: store
        folder: Store
        type: file
        allowUiUpdates: false
        options:
          path: /var/lib/grafana/dashboards
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: grafana
  labels:
    app: grafana
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: grafana
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: grafana
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 472
        runAsGroup: 472
        fsGroup: 472
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
      containers:
        - name: grafana
          image: grafana/grafana:12.1.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
          env:
            - name: GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_USER
              value: admin
            - name: GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: grafana-admin
                  key: password
            - name: GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_ENABLED
              value: "false"
            - name: GF_ANALYTICS_REPORTING_ENABLED
              value: "false"
            - name: GF_DASHBOARDS_DEFAULT_HOME_DASHBOARD_PATH
              value: /var/lib/grafana/dashboards/store.json
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /api/health
              port: 3000
            periodSeconds: 10
          resources:
            requests:
              memory: "128Mi"
              cpu: "100m"
            limits:
              memory: "384Mi"
              cpu: "500m"
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities:
              drop: [ "ALL" ]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: provisioning
              mountPath: /etc/grafana/provisioning/datasources/datasources.yaml
              subPath: datasources.yaml
            - name: provisioning
              mountPath: /etc/grafana/provisioning/dashboards/dashboards.yaml
              subPath: dashboards.yaml
            - name: dashboards
              mountPath: /var/lib/grafana/dashboards
            - name: data
              mountPath: /var/lib/grafana
            - name: tmp
              mountPath: /tmp
      volumes:
        - name: provisioning
          configMap:
            name: grafana-provisioning
        - name: dashboards
          configMap:
            name: grafana-dashboards
        - name: data
          emptyDir: {}
        - name: tmp
          emptyDir: {}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: grafana
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: grafana
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 3000
      targetPort: 3000

docs.title: Authorization (RBAC)
docs.text: Owner: Nicolas

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
The gateway already guaranteed who the user is (valid JWT → id-account header), but not what they could do. Anyone with an account, logged in with their own token, could do the following through the gateway:

Request What happened GET /accounts listed all accounts, with everyone's name and email GET /accounts/{id de outro} saw someone else's account DELETE /accounts/{id de outro} deleted someone else's account POST /accounts/login used an internal route, meant only for Auth

This is the Authentication & Authorization bottleneck from the course table: access control is missing. The suggested mitigation is RBAC (role-based access control): each account has a role and permissions depend on the role.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Two roles, USER and ADMIN. The role lives in Account, travels inside the signed JWT and is checked at the gateway, the single entry point:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor u as User
    participant gw as gateway
    participant auth as auth
    participant acc as account
    u->>auth: POST /auth/login
    auth->>acc: POST /accounts/login
    acc-->>auth: id, name, email, role
    auth-->>u: cookie with the JWT (role claim)
    u->>gw: GET /accounts (cookie)
    gw->>auth: POST /auth/solve (or Redis cache)
    auth-->>gw: idAccount + role
    alt role not allowed
        gw-->>u: 403 Forbidden
    else role allowed
        gw->>acc: forwards with id-account
        acc-->>u: 200
    end

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
Route chosen by the gateway USER ADMIN account (/accounts/**) only GET /accounts/{o próprio id} everything auth, exchange and the others everything (being authenticated is enough) everything open routes (register, login, logout) no token no token

No token or an invalid token is still 401; a valid token without permission is 403.

docs.title: Where each part lives
docs.text: Repository Change account AccountOut gained the role field account-service role column (NOT NULL DEFAULT 'USER', CHECK only USER/ADMIN) in migration V2026.11.16.001__add_role.sql; every account created is USER, and the role is never read from the request auth-service role claim in the JWT; POST /auth/solve returns idAccount and role; tests in JwtServiceTest gateway-service AccessPolicy (the rules above), called by AuthorizationFilter after validating the token; the Redis cache now stores id papel

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text: Decision Reason Role in the JWT, checked at the gateway The gateway already resolves the token on every request (with a cache): the check adds no network call. The services stay simple and only receive what they are allowed to receive. The rule looks at the route chosen by the gateway, not the URL text Variations such as /accounts;x=1, /accounts/ or %34%32 land on the same route and the same rule. Comparing URL strings would leave gaps. Deny by default in account USER has a single exception (their own account). Anything else, including a new route that account may gain, requires ADMIN without anyone having to remember to update the rule. The "owner" is compared with the decoded, parameter-free segment, and only on an exact /accounts/{id} /accounts/42/x, /accounts/42;x=1 and /accounts/42/../43 are denied. A new account is always USER; ADMIN only directly in the database Nobody can promote themselves through the API: a "role": "ADMIN" in the sign-up body is ignored (tested). A token without the role claim (issued before RBAC) counts as USER When in doubt, the least access. An old value in the cache (id only) counts as a miss and is resolved again. Metric gateway_rbac_decision_total{result=allow\|deny} Shows in Prometheus how many requests RBAC blocked.

docs.title: Promote an account to ADMIN
docs.text:
There is no route for this, on purpose. On compose:

docker compose exec db sh -c 'psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" \
  -c "UPDATE accounts.accounts SET role = '"'ADMIN'"' WHERE email = '"'admin@exemplo.com'"'"'

The new role takes effect from the next login, because the role that counts is the one in the token.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
Tested on local compose (16/11/2026), with two new accounts (Ana and Bruno):

Test Expected Got Bruno's sign-up with "role": "ADMIN" in the body USER account USER Ana (USER): GET /accounts 403 403 Ana (USER): GET /accounts/{própria} 200 200 Ana (USER): GET /accounts/{Bruno} 403 403 Ana (USER): DELETE /accounts/{Bruno} 403 403 Ana (USER): GET /accounts;x=1 403 403 Ana (USER): GET /auth/me 200 200 Ana promoted in the database, still with the old token: GET /accounts 403 403 Ana (ADMIN, new login): GET /accounts 200 200 Ana (ADMIN): DELETE /accounts/{Bruno} 204 204
  • scripts/smoke-test.sh gained the three RBAC checks (USER listing, viewing someone else's account and deleting → 403) and passed in full.
  • Automated tests: 9 new ones in the gateway (GatewayRoutingTest, AccessPolicyTest, TokenCacheTest), 31 in total, and 4 in auth-service (JwtServiceTest, including swapping USER for ADMIN in the payload, which invalidates the signature → 401). All pass in CI.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text: Limitation How it would look in production Demoting an ADMIN only takes effect when their token expires (up to 1 h) short-lived token with a refresh token, or a revocation list checked by the gateway Only two fixed roles, no fine-grained permissions roles with permissions (e.g. accounts:read, accounts:delete) or an OAuth2/OIDC server (Keycloak, Cognito) Promotion to ADMIN is manual, in the database an administrative route with auditing, protected by RBAC itself The check happens only at the gateway inside the cluster, services trust whoever calls them (they are ClusterIP). In production, network policies or mTLS between services

docs.title: Vulnerability scanning
docs.text: Owner: Leonardo

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Each service pulls in hundreds of dependencies (Spring, Netty, Jackson…) and runs in an image with a whole operating system. A CVE in any of them, a secret left behind in the code or a permissive k8s manifest becomes an entry point — and nobody reviews that manually on every commit.

docs.title: Solution: three automatic layers
docs.text:
Layer Tool Where it runs What it catches SCA + secrets + IaC (code) Trivy fs each service's pipeline, on every push/PR CVEs in the pom.xml/requirements.txt dependencies, secrets in the repository, misconfig in Dockerfile and k8s/*.yaml Image Trivy image each service's pipeline, before the push CVEs in the image's OS packages and in the jars/libs inside it DAST (running application) OWASP ZAP baseline integration workflow of platform Security headers, cookies, information leakage, gateway responses through Nginx Registry ECR scan on push AWS, on every pushed image Second opinion on the already published image 
flowchart LR
    push([git push]) --> build[mvn verify]
    build --> fs["Trivy fs<br/>deps · secrets · Dockerfile · k8s"]
    fs --> img["docker build<br/>+ Trivy image"]
    img --> gate{"Fixable CRITICAL<br/>or secret?"}
    gate -- yes --> fail([pipeline fails])
    gate -- no --> pub["push GHCR / ECR"] --> deploy[deploy EKS]
    fs & img -.SARIF.-> sec[(GitHub<br/>Security tab)]

docs.title: Gate policy
docs.text:
• Fails the pipeline: a CRITICAL vulnerability with an available fix (--ignore-unfixed) or any secret found.
  • Reports without failing: HIGH and MEDIUM, and misconfigurations. Everything goes to the Security → Code scanning tab of each repository (SARIF), to the job summary and to a trivy-<serviço> artifact.
  • Accepted findings go in the repository's .trivyignore, with the justification next to them.

docs.title: Supply chain of the scanner itself
docs.text: Supply chain attacks have already repointed tags of popular GitHub Actions to malicious code (the best-known case is tj-actions/changed-files, in 2025). That is why the pipeline does not use the Trivy action: it runs the official image pinned by digest (aquasec/trivy@sha256:…, version 0.76.1), and the ZAP action is pinned by commit SHA. A digest/SHA cannot be repointed; a tag can.

docs.title: What the scan found (and what was fixed)
docs.text:
First scan of gateway-service:

Finding Severity Action pom.xml dependencies (Spring Boot 4.1.2, Spring Cloud 2025.1.4) — 0 CVEs eclipse-temurin:25 image (full JDK) — replaced with eclipse-temurin:25-jre: fewer packages; the final image has 0 HIGH/CRITICAL (8 MEDIUM from Ubuntu, no critical fix) DS-0002: container runs as root HIGH USER 1001 in the Dockerfile KSV-0014: writable root filesystem HIGH readOnlyRootFilesystem: true + emptyDir on /tmp KSV-0118 / KSV-0104: default securityContext, no seccomp HIGH / MEDIUM runAsNonRoot, seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault, capabilities.drop: [ALL], allowPrivilegeEscalation: false KSV-0013: :latest tag in the manifest MEDIUM accepted: CI replaces it with the commit tag before kubectl apply (.trivyignore) KSV-0125: untrusted registry (ghcr.io) MEDIUM accepted: it is the org's own registry (.trivyignore) KSV-01010: ConfigMap with sensitive content MEDIUM false positive: internal URLs only (.trivyignore)

After the fixes: 0 findings in the code and 0 HIGH/CRITICAL in the image.

In the account-service and auth-service repositories the scan found no CVEs in the dependencies; the only finding is the same DS-0002 (Dockerfile runs as root), suggested in each one's CI PR.

api/gateway-service/.trivyignore
# Achados do Trivy aceitos conscientemente (revisar a cada entrega).

# k8s/k8s.yaml usa ":latest" só como base: no deploy o CI troca pela tag do
# commit (sha-xxxxxxx) antes do kubectl apply.
KSV-0013

# ghcr.io/pna26 é o registry da própria organização (ou o ECR do grupo, no CI).
KSV-0125

# Falso positivo: a ConfigMap só tem URLs internas (AUTH_URI etc.), nenhum segredo.
KSV-01010

docs.title: OWASP ZAP (DAST)
docs.text:
The integration workflow brings up the whole platform with compose and runs the ZAP baseline against http://localhost:8080 — that is, through Nginx, like a user. The report (HTML/Markdown/JSON) is kept as the job's zap-report artifact. The tuned rules live in .zap/rules.tsv:

.zap/rules.tsv
10049   IGNORE  (Non Storable Content) API JSON sem cache, esperado
10021   WARN    (X-Content-Type-Options Header Missing)
10038   WARN    (Content Security Policy Header Not Set)

docs.title: Pipeline excerpt
docs.text:
.github/workflows/service.yaml (excerpt)
      # ---------------------------------------------------------- scan: código
      - name: Data (chave do cache do Trivy)
        id: date
        run: echo "today=$(date -u +%F)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Cache do banco do Trivy
        uses: actions/cache@v6
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/trivy
          key: trivy-db-${{ steps.date.outputs.today }}
          restore-keys: trivy-db-

      - name: Trivy - código (dependências, segredos, Dockerfile e k8s)
        run: |
          mkdir -p ~/.cache/trivy ~/.m2 reports
          # .trivyignore é opcional (achados aceitos, com justificativa)
          IGNORE=(); [ -f .trivyignore ] && IGNORE=(--ignorefile /src/.trivyignore)
          docker run --rm \
            -v "$PWD:/src" -v "$HOME/.m2:/root/.m2:ro" -v "$HOME/.cache/trivy:/root/.cache/trivy" \
            "$TRIVY_IMAGE" fs /src \
              --scanners vuln,secret,misconfig \
              --severity MEDIUM,HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed \
              --skip-dirs /src/target --skip-dirs /src/reports \
              "${IGNORE[@]}" \
              --offline-scan \
              --db-repository "$TRIVY_DB" --java-db-repository "$TRIVY_JAVA_DB" \
              --format json --output /src/reports/trivy-fs.json

      - name: Trivy - imagem (build local)
        if: inputs.image != ''
        id: localimage

docs.title: AWS
docs.text:
Owner: Nicolas

This page covers the AWS account foundation: region, cost alert, command-line access, the image repositories (ECR) and the role GitHub Actions uses to sign in to AWS without an access key. The cluster and the database are covered in EKS; the network (VPC, subnets, NAT) is created together with the cluster by eksctl.

flowchart LR
    subgraph gh[GitHub · org pna26]
        ci[GitHub Actions<br/>service.yaml]
    end
    subgraph aws[Account 637423273088 · us-east-2]
        oidc[OIDC provider<br/>token.actions.githubusercontent.com]
        role[IAM role<br/>github-actions-pna26]
        ecr[(ECR<br/>5 repositories)]
        eks[EKS eks-store]
        budget[budget pna26-mensal<br/>US$ 20/month]
    end
    ci -->|"1. OIDC token signed by GitHub"| oidc
    oidc -->|"2. checks aud and sub"| role
    role -->|"3. temporary credentials (1 h)"| ci
    ci -->|"image push"| ecr
    ci -->|"kubectl apply (access entry)"| eks
    eks -.->|"pull"| ecr

docs.title: Account and region
docs.text:
Item Value Account 637423273088 (provided by the course) People's access IAM Identity Center (SSO), AdministratorAccess role Region for everything us-east-2 (Ohio) Tools AWS CLI 2, eksctl, kubectl

Why us-east-2: it has every service we use (EKS, RDS, ECR) at the same prices as us-east-1, and a single region avoids forgotten resources elsewhere generating costs. All configuration (cluster, ECR, CI's AWS_REGION variable) uses this region.

docs.title: Course guide and what we did
docs.text:
The course's AWS guide suggests creating an IAM user, signing in to the console, generating an access key and configuring the AWS CLI with it. We followed the same steps, replacing the long-lived key with SSO login:

Course step What we did Why 1. Create user the course account already comes with IAM Identity Center; each person signs in with their own SSO user no IAM user needed 2. Sign in to the console SSO portal → account 637423273088 → AdministratorAccess role — 3. Create access key we did not create one an access key stays valid until someone revokes it; if it leaks (in a commit, in a screenshot), it grants access to the account. SSO issues temporary credentials that expire on their own 4. Configure the AWS CLI aws configure sso (default profile, region us-east-2) the CLI uses the same temporary SSO credentials

The same principle applies to CI: instead of storing an access key in GitHub, it uses the OIDC role.

aws configure sso          # uma vez: portal do SSO, conta, papel e região us-east-2
aws sso login              # quando a sessão expira
aws sts get-caller-identity

docs.title: Cost alert
docs.text:
The first step, before creating any resource, was a budget in AWS Budgets:

Setting Value Name pna26-mensal Limit US$ 20 per month (actual cost) Email alerts 85% and 100% of actual spend; 100% of forecasted spend for the month

The budget only alerts, it does not block: AWS keeps charging after the limit. That is why the EKS environment is deleted when not in use (see EKS costs). The forecast alert is the most useful one: it fires early in the month if the spending pace is going to exceed the limit, before the money is spent.

docs.title: ECR
docs.text:
One repository per image, with the same name the pipeline uses:

Repository Image gateway-service gateway (Java) auth-service auth (Java) account-service account (Java) exchange-service exchange (Python) notification-service messaging consumer

Address: 637423273088.dkr.ecr.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/<repositório>:<tag>.

Decision Reason ECR (not just GHCR) for EKS The org's GHCR packages are private. EKS nodes already have read permission on the account's own ECR, with no pull secret needed. Scan on push enabled ECR scans every pushed image for CVEs, a second opinion on top of CI's Trivy. *-service names These are the names service.yaml already used; so no pipeline had to change.

docs.title: GitHub Actions role (OIDC)
docs.text:
CI needs to push images to ECR and deploy to EKS. The usual approach would be to create an IAM user and store its access key as a GitHub secret. We did not do that: a long-lived key is valid forever until someone revokes it, and if it leaks (log, fork, public repository) it grants access to the account.

Instead, AWS trusts GitHub as an identity provider (OIDC):

  1. the job requests an OIDC token from GitHub (that is why ci.yaml needs id-token: write); the token is signed by GitHub and states which repository, branch and workflow it came from;
  2. the aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials action exchanges that token for temporary credentials (sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity) of the github-actions-pna26 role;
  3. AWS only accepts it if the role's conditions match; the credentials expire in 1 hour.
Component Value OIDC provider token.actions.githubusercontent.com, audience sts.amazonaws.com Role arn:aws:iam::637423273088:role/github-actions-pna26 Who can assume it tokens whose sub starts with repo:pna26@317011053/ (any repository in the org) What it can do ECR login; push/pull only to the 5 repositories above; eks:DescribeCluster Inside the cluster access entry with AmazonEKSAdminPolicy + RoleBinding to the admin role, only in the store namespace (see EKS) Trust (who can assume it)Permissions (what it can do) 
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::637423273088:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com"
        },
        "StringLike": {
          "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:pna26@317011053/*"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "EcrLogin",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "ecr:GetAuthorizationToken",
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "EcrPushPull",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "ecr:DescribeRepositories",
        "ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability",
        "ecr:BatchGetImage",
        "ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer",
        "ecr:InitiateLayerUpload",
        "ecr:UploadLayerPart",
        "ecr:CompleteLayerUpload",
        "ecr:PutImage"
      ],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:ecr:us-east-2:637423273088:repository/gateway-service",
        "arn:aws:ecr:us-east-2:637423273088:repository/auth-service",
        "arn:aws:ecr:us-east-2:637423273088:repository/account-service",
        "arn:aws:ecr:us-east-2:637423273088:repository/exchange-service",
        "arn:aws:ecr:us-east-2:637423273088:repository/notification-service"
      ]
    },
    {
      "Sid": "EksDescribe",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "eks:DescribeCluster",
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}

Permissions follow least privilege: the role neither creates nor deletes AWS resources, does not read other ECR repositories and, in Kubernetes, only touches the store namespace. Creating the cluster, RDS and the Secrets remains a manual step, done with a person's SSO login.

The role ARN, region and namespace live in GitHub organization variables (AWS_ROLE_ARN, AWS_REGION, K8S_NAMESPACE and, with the cluster up, EKS_CLUSTER), described in CI/CD. They are not secrets: without an OIDC token from an org repository, the ARN is useless.

# provedor OIDC do GitHub (uma vez por conta)
aws iam create-open-id-connect-provider \
  --url https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \

# role com a política de confiança e a de permissões

  --assume-role-policy-document file://setup/aws/github-actions-trust.json
aws iam put-role-policy --role-name github-actions-pna26 \
  --policy-name ecr-push-eks-describe \
  --policy-document file://setup/aws/github-actions-permissions.json

# repositórios do ECR, com varredura a cada push
for r in gateway-service auth-service account-service exchange-service notification-service; do
  aws ecr create-repository --repository-name $r --region us-east-2 \
    --image-scanning-configuration scanOnPush=true
done

docs.title: Issues encountered
docs.text:
Issue Cause Solution CI fails with Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity (10/11/2026, first push after enabling OIDC) the org's repositories use GitHub's immutable subject: the token's sub is repo:pna26@317011053/account-service@1443117992:ref:refs/heads/main (with the numeric ids of the org and repository), and the role's condition was repo:pna26/* condition changed to repo:pna26@317011053/*. It is even safer: the numeric id does not change, so another org that someday uses the name pna26 does not match the rule docker login to ECR fails on Windows SSO token larger than the Windows Credential Manager limit docker-credential-ecr-login (details in EKS)

A repository's sub format can be seen with gh api repos/pna26/<repositório>/actions/oidc/customization/sub.

docs.title: Possible improvements
docs.text: Improvement Effect Restrict trust to ...:ref:refs/heads/main only pushes to main would assume the role (today, a workflow on another branch of an org repository can too) Enable secret scanning and push protection in the org GitHub blocks a push that accidentally contains an AWS key One role per repository exchange's CI would not be able to push an image to account's repository

docs.title: CI/CD (GitHub Actions)
docs.text:
Owner: Leonardo

We chose GitHub Actions over Jenkins: it needs no self-hosted server, secrets live in the GitHub organization and results show up directly in PRs and in the Security tab.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
A single reusable pipeline lives in the platform repository (.github/workflows/service.yaml) and each microservice only has a small file that calls it. A fix to the pipeline applies to every service at once.

flowchart LR
    subgraph svc ["service repo (push/PR)"]
        ci["ci.yaml<br/>(10 lines)"]
    end
    subgraph platform ["pna26/platform"]
        reuse["service.yaml<br/>(workflow_call)"]
    end
    ci -->|uses| reuse
    reuse --> b["1. build + tests"]
    b --> s1["2. Trivy: code"]
    s1 --> s2["3. Trivy: image"]
    s2 --> gate{"security<br/>gate"}
    gate -->|"push to main"| p["4. multi-arch push<br/>GHCR + ECR"]
    p --> d["5. EKS deploy<br/>kubectl apply + rollout"]
Stage When What it does 1. Build and tests always mvn verify (Java, after mvn install of the org's account/auth interfaces) or pytest (Python) 2. Trivy on code always dependencies, secrets, Dockerfile and k8s/ (details) 3. Trivy on image services local docker build and image scan before publishing Gate always fails on a fixable CRITICAL CVE or an exposed secret 4. Push push to main linux/amd64 + linux/arm64 image to ghcr.io/pna26/<serviço>:sha-<commit> and :latest; also to ECR when AWS credentials are available (creates the repository with scan on push if missing) 5. Deploy push to main with EKS_CLUSTER set aws eks update-kubeconfig, swaps the :latest image in k8s/ for the commit's, kubectl apply and waits for rollout status

On pull requests only stages 1–3 run: the PR shows whether it compiles, whether tests pass and whether the scan finds anything, without publishing anything.

docs.title: AWS configuration (align with Nicolas)
docs.text:
The pipeline signs in to AWS via OIDC: the job requests a token from GitHub and assumes an IAM role, so no access key is stored in GitHub. That is why the ci.yaml of any repo that publishes an image needs id-token: write under permissions. The service.yaml jobs declare no permissions and inherit those of ci.yaml: a reusable workflow cannot have more permissions than its caller, and if it requested id-token: write, every repository without that line would lose CI. So, without the line, the pipeline runs the same, publishes only to GHCR and warns that it skipped ECR; the EKS deploy fails with a message stating what is missing. The libraries (account, auth) do not publish an image and do not need it.

Deploy only turns on when these variables exist in the pna26 organization (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → Variables), so no repository needs to change:

Variable Value AWS_ROLE_ARN arn:aws:iam::637423273088:role/github-actions-pna26 AWS_REGION us-east-2 K8S_NAMESPACE store EKS_CLUSTER eks-store (only once the cluster is up)

The role trusts the org's repositories (repo:pna26@317011053/*, see AWS) and can: push/pull to ECR (the gateway-service, auth-service, account-service and exchange-service repositories are created separately) and eks:DescribeCluster. For kubectl apply it also needs an access entry on the cluster with the AmazonEKSAdminPolicy policy on the store namespace, plus a RoleBinding to the namespace's admin role: without it Kubernetes blocks the Prometheus Role that infra applies (details in EKS).

Without AWS

Without AWS_ROLE_ARN, the pipeline still builds, tests, scans and publishes the images to GHCR. EKS can pull from GHCR as long as the packages are public.

docs.title: OIDC and ECR (10–13/11)
docs.text:
Runs on main after OIDC. In all of them, the job signed in to AWS with no key stored in GitHub (Credenciais da AWS step), logged in to ECR and published the image to ECR and GHCR. The deploy no EKS job shows as skipped because the EKS_CLUSTER variable only exists while the cluster is up.

Excerpt from the gateway log (Build e push step):

pushing manifest for 637423273088.dkr.ecr.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/gateway-service:sha-0bb8f83@sha256:55a869db80fc... done

docs.title: EKS deploy (16/11)
docs.text:
With eks-store up and EKS_CLUSTER=eks-store set in the org, the reusable pipeline ran the whole path without any manual deploy command: build, tests, Trivy, OIDC, push to ECR, swapping the :latest image for the commit's, kubectl apply and rollout status.

Workflow Run Commit Build, tests and Trivy EKS deploy account-service 43856117521 b8d85c0 auth-service 43856123470 81e9c12 notification-service 43856129429 b3dc4c6 infra (1st attempt) 43855377825 — — Kubernetes blocked Prometheus's Role (solved with a RoleBinding, see EKS) infra (2nd attempt) 43855531385 — — manifests applied and Redis ready, but lb did not come up

Gateway and exchange were not published that day. The red on infra's 2nd attempt was a problem with lb itself:

deployment "redis" successfully rolled out
Waiting for deployment "lb" rollout to finish: 0 of 2 updated replicas are available...
error: timed out waiting for the condition

Nginx resolved the gateway name only at startup and, without the gateway Service, crashed with host not found. infra stopped at lb and never got to check Prometheus and Grafana. Fix: k8s/lb.yaml now resolves the gateway at runtime (resolve, see Load balancing): lb becomes ready before the gateway, returns 502 while it does not exist and starts forwarding on its own once the gateway comes up. Tested in a container with the same nginx.conf: without gateway, /lb/health → 200 and / → 502; the gateway comes up and / turns 200 without restarting Nginx.

Next time the cluster comes up

The CI deploy of gateway and exchange, and a green infra with the lb fix, are left for the next time the cluster comes up: one Run workflow for each, with the run link here.
