docs.title: Full pipeline
docs.text:
.github/workflows/service.yaml 
# Pipeline de CI/CD reutilizável por TODOS os microsserviços da pna26.
#
# Cada repositório só precisa de um .github/workflows/ci.yaml pequeno que chama
# este arquivo (exemplo em docs/devops/ci-cd.md). Etapas:
#
#   1. build + testes          (mvn verify | pytest)
#   2. Trivy no código         (dependências, segredos e misconfig de Dockerfile/k8s)
#   3. build da imagem + Trivy na imagem (SO + jar/libs)
#   4. push multi-arch         (GHCR sempre; ECR quando a org tiver AWS_ROLE_ARN)
#   5. deploy no EKS           (kubectl apply do k8s/ do repo + rollout)
#
# A AWS é acessada via OIDC: o job assume a role vars.AWS_ROLE_ARN, sem chave
# de acesso guardada no GitHub. Para isso o ci.yaml de quem chama precisa dar
# "id-token: write". Os jobs daqui não declaram "permissions" e herdam as de quem
# chama: se pedissem id-token e o ci.yaml não desse, o pipeline nem começaria
# (o reutilizável não pode ter mais permissão que quem chama). Sem id-token, o
# pipeline roda igual e publica só no GHCR; o ECR e o deploy no EKS precisam dele.
#
# 4 e 5 só rodam em push na main. O pipeline falha se o Trivy achar
# vulnerabilidade CRITICAL com correção disponível ou um segredo no código.

name: service

on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      service:
        description: 'Nome do Deployment/container no Kubernetes (ex.: gateway)'
        type: string
        required: true
      image:
        description: 'Nome da imagem no registry (ex.: gateway-service). Vazio = biblioteca (sem imagem/deploy)'
        type: string
        default: ''
      language:
        description: 'java | python'
        type: string
        default: java
      maven-deps:
        description: 'Repos de interface da org para "mvn install" antes do build (ex. "account auth")'
        type: string
        default: ''
      aws-region:
        type: string
        default: ''
      eks-cluster:
        description: 'Nome do cluster EKS. Vazio = não faz deploy'
        type: string
        default: ''
      k8s-namespace:
        type: string
        default: store
      fail-on-critical:
        description: 'Falhar o pipeline com CVE CRITICAL corrigível ou segredo exposto'
        type: boolean
        default: true
    outputs:
      image:
        description: 'Imagem publicada (registry/nome:sha-xxxxxxx)'
        value: ${{ jobs.build.outputs.image }}

env:
  # Trivy 0.76.1 fixado por digest (não por tag): uma tag pode ser reapontada
  # num ataque de supply chain, o digest não
  TRIVY_IMAGE: aquasec/trivy@sha256:790fd66d1697395d8693d1acaa1ea702406a20f109b6fc7bac8db623eca6c06c
  TRIVY_DB: public.ecr.aws/aquasecurity/trivy-db,ghcr.io/aquasecurity/trivy-db
  TRIVY_JAVA_DB: public.ecr.aws/aquasecurity/trivy-java-db,ghcr.io/aquasecurity/trivy-java-db

jobs:

  build:
    name: build, testes e scan
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # sem "permissions": herda as do ci.yaml (contents: read, packages: write,
    # security-events: write e, se houver, id-token: write); ver o cabeçalho
    outputs:
      image: ${{ steps.publish.outputs.image }}
    env:
      IMAGE_NAME: ${{ inputs.image }}
      PUBLISH: ${{ inputs.image != '' && github.event_name != 'pull_request' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' }}
      HAS_AWS: ${{ vars.AWS_ROLE_ARN != '' && inputs.aws-region != '' }}
    steps:

      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # O runner só expõe ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL quando o ci.yaml dá "id-token: write"
      - name: OIDC disponível?
        run: |
          if [ -n "${ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL:-}" ]; then
            echo "OIDC=true" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
            echo "id-token: write concedido pelo ci.yaml (OIDC disponível)"
          else
            echo "OIDC=false" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
            echo "sem id-token: write no ci.yaml (OIDC indisponível)"
            if [ "$PUBLISH" = true ] && [ "$HAS_AWS" = true ]; then
              echo "::warning::o ci.yaml deste repositório não dá \"id-token: write\": a imagem vai só para o GHCR, sem ECR"
            fi
          fi

      # ---------------------------------------------------------------- build
      - name: Java 25
        if: inputs.language == 'java'
        uses: actions/setup-java@v6
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: '25'
          cache: maven

      - name: Interfaces da org (mvn install)
        if: inputs.language == 'java' && inputs.maven-deps != ''
        env:
          DEPS: ${{ inputs.maven-deps }}
        run: |
          for dep in $DEPS; do
            echo "::group::mvn install $dep"
            git clone --depth 1 "https://github.com/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY_OWNER}/${dep}.git" "$RUNNER_TEMP/$dep"
            mvn -B -q -f "$RUNNER_TEMP/$dep/pom.xml" install -DskipTests
            echo "::endgroup::"
          done

      - name: Build e testes (mvn verify)
        if: inputs.language == 'java'
        run: mvn -B verify

      - name: Python 3.12
        if: inputs.language == 'python'
        uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'

      - name: Dependências e testes (pytest)
        if: inputs.language == 'python'
        run: |
          [ -f requirements.txt ] && pip install -r requirements.txt
          pip install pytest
          # o pytest devolve 5 quando não acha nenhum teste: vira só um aviso
          set +e; pytest -q; rc=$?; set -e
          [ "$rc" -eq 5 ] && { echo "::warning::nenhum teste encontrado"; exit 0; }
          exit "$rc"

      # ---------------------------------------------------------- scan: código
      - name: Data (chave do cache do Trivy)
        id: date
        run: echo "today=$(date -u +%F)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Cache do banco do Trivy
        uses: actions/cache@v6
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/trivy
          key: trivy-db-${{ steps.date.outputs.today }}
          restore-keys: trivy-db-

      - name: Trivy - código (dependências, segredos, Dockerfile e k8s)
        run: |
          mkdir -p ~/.cache/trivy ~/.m2 reports
          # .trivyignore é opcional (achados aceitos, com justificativa)
          IGNORE=(); [ -f .trivyignore ] && IGNORE=(--ignorefile /src/.trivyignore)
          docker run --rm \
            -v "$PWD:/src" -v "$HOME/.m2:/root/.m2:ro" -v "$HOME/.cache/trivy:/root/.cache/trivy" \
            "$TRIVY_IMAGE" fs /src \
              --scanners vuln,secret,misconfig \
              --severity MEDIUM,HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed \
              --skip-dirs /src/target --skip-dirs /src/reports \
              "${IGNORE[@]}" \
              --offline-scan \
              --db-repository "$TRIVY_DB" --java-db-repository "$TRIVY_JAVA_DB" \
              --format json --output /src/reports/trivy-fs.json

      - name: Trivy - imagem (build local)
        if: inputs.image != ''
        id: localimage
        run: |
          docker build -t "local/$IMAGE_NAME:scan" .
          IGNORE=(); [ -f .trivyignore ] && IGNORE=(--ignorefile /src/.trivyignore)
          docker run --rm \
            -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
            -v "$PWD:/src" -v "$HOME/.cache/trivy:/root/.cache/trivy" \
            "$TRIVY_IMAGE" image "local/$IMAGE_NAME:scan" \
              --scanners vuln,secret \
              --severity MEDIUM,HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed \
              "${IGNORE[@]}" \
              --db-repository "$TRIVY_DB" --java-db-repository "$TRIVY_JAVA_DB" \
              --format json --output /src/reports/trivy-image.json

      - name: Relatório do Trivy (resumo do job + SARIF)
        if: always()
        run: |
          shopt -s nullglob
          {
            echo "## Trivy - varredura de vulnerabilidades"
            echo
            echo "| Alvo | Tipo | CRITICAL | HIGH | MEDIUM | Segredos | Misconfig |"
            echo "|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|"
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          for report in reports/trivy-*.json; do
            jq -r '.Results[]? | [
                .Target, .Type,
                ([.Vulnerabilities[]? | select(.Severity=="CRITICAL")] | length),
                ([.Vulnerabilities[]? | select(.Severity=="HIGH")] | length),
                ([.Vulnerabilities[]? | select(.Severity=="MEDIUM")] | length),
                (.Secrets // [] | length),
                ([.Misconfigurations[]? | select(.Status=="FAIL")] | length)
              ] | "| " + (map(tostring) | join(" | ")) + " |"' "$report" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
            name=$(basename "$report" .json)
            docker run --rm -v "$PWD/reports:/reports" "$TRIVY_IMAGE" \
              convert --format sarif --output "/reports/$name.sarif" "/reports/$name.json"
            docker run --rm -v "$PWD/reports:/reports" "$TRIVY_IMAGE" \
              convert --format table "/reports/$name.json" || true
          done

      - name: Enviar para a aba Security (código)
        if: always() && hashFiles('reports/trivy-fs.sarif') != ''
        continue-on-error: true
        uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v4
        with:
          sarif_file: reports/trivy-fs.sarif
          category: trivy-fs

      - name: Enviar para a aba Security (imagem)
        if: always() && hashFiles('reports/trivy-image.sarif') != ''
        continue-on-error: true
        uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v4
        with:
          sarif_file: reports/trivy-image.sarif
          category: trivy-image

      - name: Guardar relatórios
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: trivy-${{ inputs.service }}
          path: reports/
          if-no-files-found: ignore

      - name: Portão de segurança (CRITICAL corrigível ou segredo = falha)
        if: inputs.fail-on-critical
        run: |
          shopt -s nullglob
          total=0
          for report in reports/trivy-*.json; do
            n=$(jq '[.Results[]? | ((.Vulnerabilities // []) | map(select(.Severity=="CRITICAL")) | length) + ((.Secrets // []) | length)] | add // 0' "$report")
            echo "$report: $n achado(s) bloqueante(s)"
            total=$((total + n))
          done
          if [ "$total" -gt 0 ]; then
            echo "::error::Trivy encontrou $total vulnerabilidade(s) CRITICAL com correção ou segredo(s) exposto(s)"
            exit 1
          fi

      # ------------------------------------------------------ publicar imagem
      - name: QEMU (build multi-arch)
        if: env.PUBLISH == 'true'
        uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@v4

      - name: Buildx
        if: env.PUBLISH == 'true'
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4

      - name: Login no GHCR
        if: env.PUBLISH == 'true'
        uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Credenciais da AWS
        if: env.PUBLISH == 'true' && env.HAS_AWS == 'true' && env.OIDC == 'true'
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
        with:
          role-to-assume: ${{ vars.AWS_ROLE_ARN }}
          aws-region: ${{ inputs.aws-region }}

      - name: Login no ECR (e cria o repositório se faltar)
        if: env.PUBLISH == 'true' && env.HAS_AWS == 'true' && env.OIDC == 'true'
        id: ecr
        run: |
          # a role do CI pode ter só push/pull (sem Describe/CreateRepository):
          # nesse caso o repositório tem que existir e o push segue normalmente
          if ! aws ecr describe-repositories --repository-names "$IMAGE_NAME" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            aws ecr create-repository --repository-name "$IMAGE_NAME" \
              --image-scanning-configuration scanOnPush=true >/dev/null 2>&1 || \
              echo "::warning::não deu para conferir/criar o repositório $IMAGE_NAME no ECR; ele precisa já existir"
          fi
          registry="$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text).dkr.ecr.${AWS_REGION}.amazonaws.com"
          aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin "$registry"
          echo "registry=$registry" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Tags
        if: env.PUBLISH == 'true'
        id: tags
        env:
          ECR: ${{ steps.ecr.outputs.registry }}
          OWNER: ${{ github.repository_owner }}
        run: |
          short="sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7}"
          tags="ghcr.io/${OWNER,,}/$IMAGE_NAME:$short,ghcr.io/${OWNER,,}/$IMAGE_NAME:latest"
          deploy="ghcr.io/${OWNER,,}/$IMAGE_NAME:$short"
          if [ -n "$ECR" ]; then
            tags="$tags,$ECR/$IMAGE_NAME:$short,$ECR/$IMAGE_NAME:latest"
            deploy="$ECR/$IMAGE_NAME:$short"
          fi
          echo "tags=$tags" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "deploy=$deploy" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Build e push (linux/amd64 + linux/arm64)
        if: env.PUBLISH == 'true'
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
          push: true
          tags: ${{ steps.tags.outputs.tags }}
          labels: |
            org.opencontainers.image.source=${{ github.server_url }}/${{ github.repository }}
            org.opencontainers.image.revision=${{ github.sha }}
          cache-from: type=gha,scope=${{ inputs.image }}
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max,scope=${{ inputs.image }}

      - name: Imagem publicada
        if: env.PUBLISH == 'true'
        id: publish
        env:
          IMAGE: ${{ steps.tags.outputs.deploy }}
        run: |
          echo "image=$IMAGE" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "### Imagem publicada: \`$IMAGE\`" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

  deploy:
    name: deploy no EKS
    needs: build
    if: >-
      inputs.image != '' && inputs.eks-cluster != '' &&
      github.event_name != 'pull_request' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # sem "permissions": herda as do ci.yaml, como o build (ver o cabeçalho)
    concurrency:
      group: deploy-${{ inputs.service }}
      cancel-in-progress: false
    env:
      SERVICE: ${{ inputs.service }}
      IMAGE_NAME: ${{ inputs.image }}
      IMAGE: ${{ needs.build.outputs.image }}
      NAMESPACE: ${{ inputs.k8s-namespace }}
      CLUSTER: ${{ inputs.eks-cluster }}
      HAS_AWS: ${{ vars.AWS_ROLE_ARN != '' && inputs.aws-region != '' }}
    steps:

      - name: Credenciais configuradas?
        if: env.HAS_AWS != 'true'
        run: |
          echo "::error::EKS_CLUSTER definido mas faltam as variáveis AWS_REGION ou AWS_ROLE_ARN na org"
          exit 1

      - name: OIDC disponível?
        run: |
          if [ -z "${ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL:-}" ]; then
            echo "::error::o deploy assume a role da AWS via OIDC: o ci.yaml deste repositório precisa de \"id-token: write\" em permissions"
            exit 1
          fi

      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
        with:
          role-to-assume: ${{ vars.AWS_ROLE_ARN }}
          aws-region: ${{ inputs.aws-region }}

      - name: kubeconfig do cluster
        run: |
          aws eks update-kubeconfig --name "$CLUSTER" --region "$AWS_REGION"
          kubectl get namespace "$NAMESPACE" >/dev/null 2>&1 || kubectl create namespace "$NAMESPACE"

      - name: kubectl apply
        run: |
          if [ ! -d k8s ]; then
            echo "::notice::este repositório não tem k8s/: nada para aplicar"
            exit 0
          fi
          # troca a imagem base (:latest) pela imagem do commit
          sed -i -E "s#(image:[[:space:]]*)[^[:space:]]*/${IMAGE_NAME}:[^[:space:]]+#\1${IMAGE}#" k8s/*.y*ml
          grep -n "image:" k8s/*.y*ml
          kubectl apply -n "$NAMESPACE" -f k8s/
          kubectl rollout status "deployment/$SERVICE" -n "$NAMESPACE" --timeout=300s
          kubectl get pods -n "$NAMESPACE" -l "app=$SERVICE" -o wide
          {
            echo "### Deploy no EKS"
            echo "- cluster: \`$CLUSTER\` / namespace: \`$NAMESPACE\`"
            echo "- deployment: \`$SERVICE\` -> \`$IMAGE\`"
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

docs.title: PaaS, costs and SLA
docs.text:
Owner: Gabriel

Prices checked on 05/11/2026, aligned with the real cluster on 09/11/2026

On-demand prices in us-east-2 (the eks-store region, see EKS), in USD, month = 730 h. Checked against the pricing pages for EKS, Fargate and Classic Load Balancer and with third-party calculators for EC2 (t3.medium US$ 0.0416/h) and public IPv4 (US$ 0.005/h). Prices change: for a real budget, use the AWS Pricing Calculator. Taxes and conversion to BRL are not included.

docs.title: What needs to run
docs.text:
Sum of the requests in the manifests that go to EKS (platform/k8s/ and each service's k8s/):

Component Replicas CPU (request) Memory (request) lb (Nginx) 2 2 × 50m 2 × 32 Mi gateway 2 2 × 250m 2 × 384 Mi auth, account, notification (Spring Boot) 1 + 1 + 1 3 × 100m 3 × 256 Mi exchange 2 2 × 100m 2 × 96 Mi kafka + mailpit 1 + 1 300m 800 Mi redis 1 100m 128 Mi prometheus + grafana 1 + 1 200m 384 Mi Platform ≈ 1.7 vCPU ≈ 3.0 GiB EKS system (coredns, aws-node, kube-proxy, metrics-server) ≈ 0.55 vCPU ≈ 0.4 GiB Reserved ≈ 2.25 vCPU ≈ 3.4 GiB

eks-store has 2 fixed t3.medium nodes (≈ 1.93 vCPU and ≈ 3.4 GiB allocatable each, ≈ 3.86 vCPU and ≈ 6.8 GiB in total). That leaves ≈ 1.6 vCPU: room for ≈ 6 more gateway replicas (250m each) in the HPA test. Beyond that, new pods stay Pending until there is one more node (the node group does not scale on its own: minSize = maxSize = 2).

docs.title: Cost on EKS (what we delivered)
docs.text:
Item Calculation USD/h USD/month EKS control plane (standard support) US$ 0.10/h 0.100 73.00 2 EC2 t3.medium nodes 2 × US$ 0.0416/h 0.083 60.74 NAT gateway (1, the nodes are private) US$ 0.045/h + US$ 0.045/GB 0.045 ≈ 33.30 Classic Load Balancer (lb's LoadBalancer Service) US$ 0.025/h + US$ 0.008/GB 0.025 ≈ 18.50 RDS PostgreSQL db.t4g.micro single-AZ + 20 GB gp3 US$ 0.016/h + 20 × US$ 0.115/month 0.019 ≈ 14.00 Public IPv4 (NAT + load balancer in 2 zones) 3 × US$ 0.005/h 0.015 10.95 Node disks (EBS gp3, 20 GB each) 2 × 20 GB × US$ 0.08/month 0.004 3.20 ECR (service images, ≈ 2 GB) US$ 0.10/GB/month — 0.20 Data transfer out first 100 GB/month free — 0.00 Total ≈ 0.29 ≈ 214

The EKS page gets to ≈ US$ 0.27/h by adding up the first five items; with the public IPv4 addresses and the disks, ≈ US$ 0.29/h.

Kubernetes version: the 6× trap

The control plane's US$ 0.10/h only applies while the cluster's Kubernetes version is in standard support (≈ 14 months after the version's release on EKS). After that the cluster automatically moves to extended support: US$ 0.60/h ≈ US$ 438/month, for the control plane alone. eks-store uses 1.37, in standard support until 11/2027.

The NAT gateway is the most expensive "hidden" item in small projects (≈ 15 % of the total, more than the load balancer). The group chose to pay for it so the nodes do not have public IPs; the cheap alternative would be nodes in a public subnet with a locked-down security group.

docs.title: For the project (US$ 20/month budget)
docs.text:
What costs money is uptime: ≈ US$ 0.29 per hour with everything up. With the US$ 20/month budget, that is ≈ 70 hours. The "EKS day" (tests, HPA load test and recording, ≈ 8 h) comes to ≈ US$ 2.30. Group rules:

  • bring the cluster up only to test/present and delete it at the end (eksctl delete cluster, steps on the EKS page): the control plane charges even with no pods;
  • billing alert on the account (AWS page);
  • RDS, NAT and the load balancer also charge while idle: delete them too.

docs.title: How to lower the cost in production
docs.text: Measure Savings Note Graviton nodes (t4g.medium, ARM) ≈ 20 % on nodes Our images are already multi-arch (amd64 + arm64) via the pipeline. Spot nodes up to ≈ 70 % on nodes The services are stateless with 2 replicas; they can survive losing a node. Do not use for the database. 1-year Savings Plan ≈ 30–40 % on EC2/Fargate Only once the load is stable. Scale by metric (HPA) pay for the peak only at the peak Uses the Prometheus metrics.

docs.title: PaaS: what if we didn't use Kubernetes?
docs.text:
The same containers can run on a PaaS, where the provider takes care of servers, load balancing and scaling. Comparison for the same platform (6 small containers + PostgreSQL + Redis):

Option Type Estimate USD/month Pros Cons EKS (current) Managed Kubernetes ≈ 214 Full control (network, Nginx, Prometheus, sidecars), portable, it is what the course requires US$ 73 for the control plane alone; more things to operate (nodes, upgrades, RBAC) ECS Fargate + ALB CaaS (serverless containers) ≈ 105 No nodes and no paid control plane; pay per container vCPU/GB Tied to AWS; Prometheus needs another solution (AMP or CloudWatch) AWS App Runner PaaS ≈ 120 git push/image → URL with HTTPS and automatic scaling No easy internal networking between services: the "gateway as the single entry point" becomes harder Render / Railway PaaS ≈ 60–150 Simplest of all, managed database and Redis in 1 click Cheap plans have 512 MB (too little for the JVM); less control over network and region (latency to Brazil) Heroku PaaS ≈ 100–180 Mature, good for prototypes Expensive per resource; basic dyno sleeps

How we got the Fargate number: 6 tasks × (0.25 vCPU + 0.5 GB) = 1.5 vCPU × US$ 0.04048/h + 3 GB × US$ 0.004445/h ≈ US$ 54 + ALB ≈ US$ 22 + ElastiCache cache.t4g.micro ≈ US$ 12 + RDS ≈ US$ 14.

Conclusion: for this platform (small, 3 developers, low load), a PaaS or Fargate would be cheaper and require less operation than EKS — most of the EKS cost is fixed (control plane + always-on nodes). EKS starts to pay off when there are many services sharing the same nodes, when you need Kubernetes features (HPA on custom metrics, service mesh, operators, multi-cloud portability) or when the team already has cluster operations figured out. We chose EKS because it is the goal of the course and because it keeps the same design (Nginx → gateway → services, shared Redis, Prometheus) as the local environment.

docs.title: SLA and SLO
docs.text: SLA is the provider's contractual commitment (with credits if not met); SLO is the internal target we set for our platform; SLI is the measurement that shows whether we met it.

docs.title: SLA of the AWS services we use
docs.text: Service Monthly SLA EKS (control plane) 99.95 % EC2 — region (instances in ≥ 2 zones) 99.99 % EC2 — single instance 99.5 % Elastic Load Balancing 99.99 % RDS single-AZ / Multi-AZ 99.5 % / 99.95 % Exchange rate API (AwesomeAPI) none (free service)

docs.title: Composite availability
docs.text:
An authenticated request goes in series through load balancer → Nginx → gateway → Auth/Account → database; the availability of the path is the product of the availabilities. Components with replicas in different zones are in parallel: 1 − (1 − 0,995)² = 99,9975 %.

Scenario Calculation Availability Downtime/month As is (2 replicas in 2 zones, RDS single-AZ) 0.9995 (EKS) × 0.9999 (ELB) × 0.99998 (nodes) × 0.995 (RDS) ≈ 99.44 % ≈ 4 h With RDS Multi-AZ … × 0.9995 ≈ 99.89 % ≈ 48 min Everything with 1 replica, 1 node 0.9995 × 0.9999 × 0.995 × 0.995 ≈ 98.95 % ≈ 7.7 h

The single-AZ database is the weakest link: gateway and Exchange replicas do not help if PostgreSQL goes down. Routes that do not depend on the database (exchange rate with a token already cached in Redis) stay up. Exchange depends on an API with no SLA; the cache with stale-if-error (Quote cache) covers up to 10 min of it being down. In eks-store, egress to AwesomeAPI still goes through the single NAT gateway (in one zone only): if it or the zone goes down, Exchange loses the external API, but the rest of the platform stays up, because no other route depends on the internet. And in Nicolas's test AwesomeAPI returned 429 to the AWS IP: the free limit is per IP, and the NAT IP is shared by all pods. That is why Exchange switched to the Central Bank's PTAX (Exchange), which is public and has no such block.

docs.title: Our SLO
docs.text:
SLI SLO (30-day window) How to measure (Prometheus) Availability: % of requests without 5xx errors at the gateway 99.5 % (≈ 3 h 39 min of error budget/month) 1 - sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{application="gateway",status=~"5.."}[30d])) / sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{application="gateway"}[30d])) Latency: request p95 < 500 ms k6 in the load test; on the server, Exchange p95 from the histogram Errors under expected load < 1 % k6's http_req_failed

Verified on EKS (19/11/2026): in the load tests through the ELB, 0 errors in 379,762 requests: p95 of 254 ms with the HPA scaling the gateway from 2 to 6 replicas (100 users) and 370 ms with 200 users and 2 fixed replicas, both with ≈ 180 ms of network latency from Brazil to us-east-2. The three SLOs in the table were met. A month's availability cannot be measured in a 4 min run: it is still the composite SLA calculation above.

Why 99.5 % and not 99.9 %: with the single-AZ database, AWS itself only guarantees ≈ 99.4 % on the full path; promising more than that would be promising what the infrastructure cannot sustain. To go up to 99.9 %, the first step is RDS Multi-AZ (+ ≈ US$ 14/month), then a Grafana alert when the 5xx rate burns through the error budget faster than normal.

SLO Allowed downtime per month 99 % 7 h 18 min 99.5 % 3 h 39 min 99.9 % 43 min 49 s 99.95 % 21 min 54 s 99.99 % 4 min 23 s

docs.title: EKS
docs.text:
Owner: Nicolas

The platform runs on an Amazon EKS cluster (eks-store, region us-east-2), with the Account database on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. Everything lives in the store namespace. The cluster is created with eksctl from a versioned file (setup/eks-store.yaml) and deleted when not in use, because it is the most expensive item in the project (see Costs).

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    user([internet]) --> elb[AWS ELB<br/>Service lb · LoadBalancer]
    subgraph vpc[VPC 10.20.0.0/16 · us-east-2a and 2b]
        subgraph pub[public subnets]
            elb
            nat[NAT gateway]
        end
        subgraph priv[private subnets · 2 t3.medium nodes]
            lb[lb · Nginx ×2] --> gw[gateway ×2]
            gw <--> redis[(Redis)]
            gw --> auth & account & exchange[exchange ×2]
            auth --> account
            prom[Prometheus] --> graf[Grafana]
        end
        rds[(RDS PostgreSQL 17<br/>db.t4g.micro)]
    end
    elb --> lb
    account -->|5432| rds
    exchange --> nat --> api([AwesomeAPI])
    priv -.->|pull| ecr[(ECR)]
Component Choice Why Kubernetes version 1.37 EKS default version, in standard support until 11/2027 (versions in extended support cost 6× more per hour) Nodes 2× t3.medium (2 vCPU, 4 GiB), managed node group memory requests add up to ~2.6 GiB; 2× t3.small (~2.9 GiB usable, 11 pods per node) left no headroom for rolling updates or the load test Network eksctl's own VPC, 2 zones, nodes in private subnets only (no public IP) nodes are not exposed; only the ELB, in the public subnets, receives internet traffic Internet egress 1 NAT gateway nodes need to pull images from ECR and exchange calls AwesomeAPI; one NAT per zone would double the cost Cluster access authenticationMode: API (access entries) Kubernetes permissions granted to AWS roles without editing the aws-auth ConfigMap Images ECR (637423273088.dkr.ecr.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/<serviço>-service) GHCR packages are private; nodes already have read permission on ECR Database RDS PostgreSQL 17.11, db.t4g.micro, 20 GB gp3 the course's EKS page asks for RDS or DynamoDB; 20 GB is the RDS minimum

docs.title: Service exposure
docs.text: Only lb is type: LoadBalancer. Gateway, auth, account and exchange are ClusterIP: they are reachable only from inside the cluster, by the names gateway, auth, account and exchange on port 8080. These are the same names as in the compose file, so the Feign clients (http://account:8080, http://auth:8080) and nginx.conf work unchanged.

docs.title: Manifests
docs.text:
Each service has its own k8s/k8s.yaml in its repository (ConfigMap, Deployment and Service), and the shared infra (lb, Redis, Prometheus, Grafana) lives in platform/k8s/. Common patterns:

  • label app: <serviço>, used by the Service selector and by the pipeline's kubectl rollout;
  • CPU and memory requests/limits (Java uses -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 to respect the limit);
  • non-root container (runAsNonRoot, uid 1001), no privilege escalation, read-only file system and an emptyDir at /tmp;
  • readinessProbe/livenessProbe (account and auth use a TCP probe on 8080, because they have no Actuator);
  • image ending in /<serviço>-service:latest: the pipeline replaces it with the commit tag (sha-xxxxxxx).

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
No secret is stored in Git. The pipeline runs kubectl apply -f k8s/ on every deploy, so an example Secret inside k8s/ would overwrite the real one. Secrets are created once per cluster:

Secret Keys Used by account-secrets DATABASE_USERNAME, DATABASE_PASSWORD account (secretRef) auth-secrets JWT_SECRET_KEY auth (secretRef) notification-secrets DATABASE_USERNAME, DATABASE_PASSWORD notification (secretRef), with the same RDS user grafana-admin password Grafana (created by the infra workflow)

The database host, port and name are not secrets and live in the account-configmap ConfigMap (DATABASE_HOST = RDS endpoint).

docs.title: RDS PostgreSQL
docs.text:
Setting Value Instance rds-store, db.t4g.micro, single-AZ Storage 20 GB gp3, encrypted, storage autoscaling disabled Network subnet group rds-store (private subnets only), no public access Firewall security group rds-store: ingress only on port 5432 and only from the EKS nodes' security group (no IP range allowed) Backup 1-day retention, no deletion protection (the environment is recreated often) Schema created by account's Flyway on first boot (accounts)

The endpoint is rds-store.<id-da-conta>.us-east-2.rds.amazonaws.com: it depends only on the instance name, account and region, so it is the same every time RDS is recreated with the name rds-store. The password is random and exists only in RDS and in the account-secrets Secret.

docs.title: Deploy via CI/CD
docs.text:
The reusable pipeline (CI/CD) deploys on every push to main when the organization variable EKS_CLUSTER is set: aws eks update-kubeconfig → swap the image for the commit's → kubectl apply -n store -f k8s/ → kubectl rollout status.

GitHub Actions signs in to AWS through the OIDC role github-actions-pna26 (see AWS). Inside the cluster, it has an access entry with the AmazonEKSAdminPolicy access policy scoped to the store namespace: it can create and update Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets and also Role/RoleBinding there, and nothing outside it. AmazonEKSEditPolicy is not enough: it follows the Kubernetes edit role, which does not allow touching roles, and the infra workflow applies Prometheus's Role/RoleBinding. Since access is limited to the namespace, store is created by hand (kubectl create namespace store, in step 1 below).

The access policy alone was not enough either (found during the 16/11 deploy). When creating a Role, Kubernetes checks whether the creator already holds every permission it is granting (privilege escalation protection). That check looks only at Kubernetes' own RBAC and does not see the permissions that come from the AWS access policy. That is why the access entry also puts the role in the store-deployers group, and a RoleBinding grants that group the admin role only in the store namespace. The scope stays the same, now granted through native RBAC.

aws eks create-access-entry --cluster-name eks-store --region us-east-2 \
  --principal-arn arn:aws:iam::637423273088:role/github-actions-pna26
aws eks associate-access-policy --cluster-name eks-store --region us-east-2 \
  --principal-arn arn:aws:iam::637423273088:role/github-actions-pna26 \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:eks::aws:cluster-access-policy/AmazonEKSAdminPolicy \
  --access-scope type=namespace,namespaces=store
# RBAC nativo: sem isto o infra não consegue criar o Role do Prometheus (escalada de privilégio)
aws eks update-access-entry --cluster-name eks-store --region us-east-2 \
  --principal-arn arn:aws:iam::637423273088:role/github-actions-pna26 --kubernetes-groups store-deployers
kubectl create rolebinding ci-store-admin -n store --clusterrole=admin --group=store-deployers
# conferência: "yes" no store e "no" fora dele
kubectl auth can-i create roles -n store   --as=ci --as-group=store-deployers
kubectl auth can-i create roles -n default --as=ci --as-group=store-deployers

Automatic deploy proven (16/11/2026)

With the cluster up and the EKS_CLUSTER=eks-store variable created in the organization, CI deployed Nicolas's three services on its own: build, tests, Trivy, push to ECR, kubectl apply and rollout status, all green.

Workflow Run Result infra (1st attempt) 43855377825 failed: Kubernetes blocked the creation of Prometheus's Role (see above) infra (after the RoleBinding) 43855531385 Redis, Kafka, Mailpit, Prometheus and Grafana up; Prometheus's Role created. Only lb did not become ready, because it waits for the gateway Service account-service 43856117521 deployed to EKS ✔ auth-service 43856123470 deployed to EKS ✔ notification-service 43856129429 deployed to EKS ✔

Gateway and exchange were not published that day: each owner runs their service's CI on the day of the load test.

docs.title: Environment lifecycle
docs.text: All commands run from the root of platform, with the AWS CLI logged in (aws sso login).

docs.title: Create (~25 min)
docs.text:
# 1. cluster, VPC, NAT e nós (~15 min); já configura o kubectl e instala o metrics-server
eksctl create cluster -f setup/eks-store.yaml
kubectl create namespace store
kubectl top nodes   # metrics-server respondendo (o HPA depende dele); leva ~1 min depois do cluster
# 2. access entry do CI + RoleBinding (comandos da seção anterior)

# 3. rede do RDS: security group (5432 só dos nós) e subnet group (sub-redes privadas)
VPC=$(aws eks describe-cluster --name eks-store --query cluster.resourcesVpcConfig.vpcId --output text)
NODES_SG=$(aws eks describe-cluster --name eks-store --query cluster.resourcesVpcConfig.clusterSecurityGroupId --output text)
SUBNETS=$(aws ec2 describe-subnets --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC Name=map-public-ip-on-launch,Values=false \
  --query 'Subnets[].SubnetId' --output text)
RDS_SG=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --vpc-id $VPC --group-name rds-store \
  --description "RDS PostgreSQL: 5432 so dos nos do eks-store" --query GroupId --output text)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id $RDS_SG --protocol tcp --port 5432 --source-group $NODES_SG
aws rds create-db-subnet-group --db-subnet-group-name rds-store \
  --db-subnet-group-description "Sub-redes privadas do eks-store" --subnet-ids $SUBNETS

# 4. RDS (~10 min) e os Secrets com a mesma senha. A senha fica só num arquivo temporário
#    (permissão só do dono), nunca na tela nem na linha de comando, e o arquivo é apagado no fim.
umask 077; T=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$T"' EXIT
DB_PASS=$(openssl rand -hex 24)
cat > "$T/rds.json" <<EOF
{"DBInstanceIdentifier":"rds-store","Engine":"postgres","EngineVersion":"17.11",
 "DBInstanceClass":"db.t4g.micro","AllocatedStorage":20,"StorageType":"gp3","StorageEncrypted":true,
 "MasterUsername":"store","MasterUserPassword":"$DB_PASS","DBName":"store",
 "DBSubnetGroupName":"rds-store","VpcSecurityGroupIds":["$RDS_SG"],
 "PubliclyAccessible":false,"MultiAZ":false,"BackupRetentionPeriod":1,"DeletionProtection":false}
EOF
aws rds create-db-instance --cli-input-json "file://$T/rds.json"
printf 'DATABASE_USERNAME=store\nDATABASE_PASSWORD=%s\n' "$DB_PASS" > "$T/db.env"
printf 'JWT_SECRET_KEY=%s\n' "$(openssl rand -base64 32)" > "$T/jwt.env"
kubectl create secret generic account-secrets      -n store --from-env-file="$T/db.env"
kubectl create secret generic notification-secrets -n store --from-env-file="$T/db.env"
kubectl create secret generic auth-secrets         -n store --from-env-file="$T/jwt.env"
unset DB_PASS
aws rds wait db-instance-available --db-instance-identifier rds-store

# 5. liga o deploy automático e publica tudo pelo CI
gh variable set EKS_CLUSTER --org pna26 --body eks-store --visibility all   # gh com escopo admin:org
gh workflow run infra -R pna26/platform --ref main
for r in gateway-service auth-service account-service exchange-service notification-service; do
  gh workflow run ci -R pna26/$r --ref main
done

docs.title: Test
docs.text:
LB=$(kubectl get svc lb -n store -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].hostname}')
BASE_URL=http://$LB ./scripts/smoke-test.sh

Result on 08/11/2026: smoke test passed — register/login with an HttpOnly cookie, 401 with no token, with an invalid token and with a forged id-account, both gateway replicas responding and the actuator blocked at the lb. The only warning was the exchange rate: AwesomeAPI returns 429 for the AWS NAT IP (the free API's limit for cloud IPs), and exchange returns 503 as expected.

Result on 16/11/2026, with the deploy done by CI (gateway and exchange not published, so no ELB): through a kubectl port-forward to auth, register 200, login 200 with an HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite=None cookie, wrong password 401. Flyway created the schema in RDS, the outbox published AccountCreated to Kafka and notification-service logged the welcome email. kubectl top pods responded (metrics-server ok).

docs.title: Delete (~15 min)
docs.text:
Order matters: the ELB (created by the lb Service) and RDS live inside the eksctl VPC and prevent it from being deleted.

kubectl delete svc lb -n store
aws rds delete-db-instance --db-instance-identifier rds-store --skip-final-snapshot --delete-automated-backups
aws rds wait db-instance-deleted --db-instance-identifier rds-store
aws rds delete-db-subnet-group --db-subnet-group-name rds-store
RDS_SG=$(aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=group-name,Values=rds-store \
  --query 'SecurityGroups[0].GroupId' --output text)
aws ec2 delete-security-group --group-id $RDS_SG
eksctl delete cluster -f setup/eks-store.yaml --disable-nodegroup-eviction
gh variable delete EKS_CLUSTER --org pna26   # senão todo push na main tenta deploy num cluster que não existe

Check that nothing is still billing (every line should come back empty):

aws eks list-clusters; aws rds describe-db-instances --query 'DBInstances[].DBInstanceIdentifier'
aws elb describe-load-balancers --query 'LoadBalancerDescriptions[].LoadBalancerName'
aws ec2 describe-nat-gateways --filter Name=state,Values=available,pending --query 'NatGateways[].NatGatewayId'
aws ec2 describe-addresses --query 'Addresses[].AllocationId'
aws ec2 describe-volumes --query 'Volumes[].VolumeId'

On 16/11/2026 the environment was created, tested and deleted on the same day; the check came back empty (only the ECR images remain).

docs.title: Costs
docs.text:
On-demand prices in us-east-2, per hour with the environment running:

Item US$/h EKS control plane (standard support) 0.100 2× EC2 t3.medium 0.083 NAT gateway (excluding data) 0.045 Classic Load Balancer 0.025 RDS db.t4g.micro + 20 GB gp3 0.019 Total ~0.27

With the US$ 20/month budget, that comes to about 70 hours running. That is why the environment is created for tests, demos and the load test and deleted right afterwards. The ECR images remain (cents per month).

docs.title: Issues encountered
docs.text: Issue Cause Solution docker login to ECR fails on Windows ("O fragmento de código recebeu dados incorretos") the ECR token obtained via SSO is ~3 KB and Windows Credential Manager accepts at most 2560 bytes use docker-credential-ecr-login (ships with Docker Desktop) in credHelpers, without docker login denied when pulling images from GHCR gh token without the read:packages scope gh auth refresh -h github.com -s read:packages infra workflow fails: roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io "prometheus" is forbidden ... attempting to grant RBAC permissions not currently held Kubernetes' anti-escalation check does not see the permissions from the AWS access policy (AmazonEKSAdminPolicy) store-deployers group on the access entry + ci-store-admin RoleBinding to the admin role in store (see Deploy via CI/CD) lb in CrashLoopBackOff: host not found in upstream "gateway:8080" Nginx resolves the gateway name at startup, and the gateway Service does not exist yet normal while gateway is not published; infra's rollout status times out because of this gh variable set --org returns 403 the gh token lacks the admin:org scope gh auth refresh -h github.com -s admin:org (and --remove-scopes admin:org afterwards) aws responds Token has expired and refresh failed the SSO session expired aws sso login lb pods restart twice on the first deploy Nginx resolves gateway at startup and came up before the gateway Service existed none: on the next attempt the Service already exists exchange returns 503 on EKS AwesomeAPI returns 429 for the AWS egress IP expected exchange behavior (cache + 503); affects the load test's exchange scenario. Fix: exchange switched to BACEN's PTAX, which is public and has no cloud blocking (Exchange); confirm on the next deploy

docs.title: Load testing
docs.text:
Owner: Gabriel

Tool: k6 (Grafana Labs), running in a container — nobody in the group needs to install anything besides Docker. We chose k6 over JMeter/Locust because the test is a JavaScript file versioned in the repository, the acceptance limits (thresholds) live in the script itself, and it sends metrics straight to Prometheus, so the load shows up in the same Grafana dashboard as the server metrics.

docs.title: What is tested
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    k6([k6<br/>N virtual users]) ==> lb[lb · Nginx] ==> gw["gateway<br/>(1, 2 or 4 replicas)"]
    gw <-->|token| redis[(Redis)]
    gw --> auth & account & exchange
    exchange -->|miss| api([AwesomeAPI])
    k6 -.->|remote write| prom[(Prometheus)] --> graf[Grafana]

The script's setup() creates 20 accounts and logs in once; after that the virtual users (VUs) reuse the tokens, like real users browsing while logged in. Each VU waits 0.5–1.5 s between actions.

Scenario Requests What it exercises auth GET /auth/me + GET /accounts/{id} token validation (Redis or Auth), load balancing, Account + PostgreSQL exchange GET /exchange/USD/BRL (80 %) and EUR/BRL gateway → Exchange → quote cache / external API login POST /auth/login expensive path: password hash + JWT issuance mixed 80 % authenticated reads, 15 % exchange, 5 % login "real" store usage Profile Load shape Question it answers smoke 1 VU, 20 s Do the script and the platform work? load ramps up to VUS in 20 s, holds for DURATION, ramps down Does it handle the expected load within the SLO? stress VUS → ×2 → ×4 → ×8, 30 s each Where does it break? Which component saturates first? spike VUS/10 → spike to VUS×4 in 5 s → back Does it handle a sudden spike and recover?

Acceptance criteria (the same as the SLO), checked by k6 — it exits with code 99 if any of them is exceeded:

Metric Limit Errors (http_req_failed) < 1 % p95 / p99 latency (expected responses) < 500 ms / < 1500 ms checks (response status and content) > 99 %

docs.title: How to run
docs.text:
./scripts/build.sh && docker compose up -d --build     # plataforma + Prometheus + Grafana

./scripts/load-test.sh                                  # mixed, perfil load, 50 VUs, 1 min
SCENARIO=auth PROFILE=stress VUS=50 ./scripts/load-test.sh
SCENARIO=exchange PROFILE=spike VUS=20 ./scripts/load-test.sh
THINK=0 SCENARIO=auth PROFILE=stress VUS=25 ./scripts/load-test.sh   # sem pausa: limite de vazão
BASE_URL=http://<endereço-do-elb> ./scripts/load-test.sh   # contra o EKS

./scripts/load-matrix.sh        # todos os experimentos abaixo (~25 min) -> load/results/RESULTS.md

While it runs, open Grafana at http://localhost:3000: the Teste de carga (k6) row shows VUs, req/s and client-side p95/p99, and the rows above show what happens in each replica, in Redis and in Exchange at the same moment.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
scripts/load-matrix.sh changes one variable at a time and keeps everything else the same (Redis cache flushed before each run):

# Experiment Variable Scenario / profile Hypothesis 1 Token cache TOKEN_CACHE_ENABLED = false × true auth / load Without cache, every request calls Auth: more load on Auth and higher latency when it saturates. With cache, gateway_token_cache_total{result="miss"} stays close to 20 (one per user). 2 Gateway replicas GATEWAY_REPLICAS = 1 × 2 × 4 auth / stress More replicas delay the point where p95 blows up — until the bottleneck moves to another component (Account/PostgreSQL or the machine's own CPU). 3 Quote cache EXCHANGE_CACHE_TTL = 0 × 30 exchange / load, 10 VUs, 30 s Without cache, Exchange latency is the external API's and 429s show up; with cache, ~1 external call every 30 s per replica. Few VUs on purpose: we don't want to hammer a third-party service. 4 Real usage default configuration mixed / load Within the SLO. 5 Saturation GATEWAY_REPLICAS = 1 × 4, THINK=0 (no pause) auth / stress up to 200 VUs With pauses, experiment 2 never reaches the limit; without pauses, each VU fires as fast as possible and shows what breaks first.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Measured on 05/11/2026 with ./scripts/load-matrix.sh (experiments 3 and 5 were run again with ONLY="3 5"). Machine: Windows 11 + Docker Desktop (WSL2), 12 logical CPUs, 7.3 GiB of RAM for Docker. k6, Nginx, gateway, services, database, Prometheus and Grafana on the same machine. Latencies only for expected responses and only for the test phase (the sign-up/login in setup() is excluded).

Run Scenario Profile Max VUs Requests req/s p50 (ms) p95 (ms) p99 (ms) Errors token-cache-off auth load 50 7,416 80.8 5 12 20 0.00 % token-cache-on auth load 50 7,448 79.7 4 7 15 0.00 % replicas-1 auth stress 400 41,110 290.9 2 3 4 0.00 % replicas-2 auth stress 400 40,810 287.1 2 17 114 0.00 % replicas-4 auth stress 400 40,918 285.8 3 7 23 0.00 % exchange-cache-off exchange load 10 445 7.3 23 49 69 0.00 % exchange-cache-on exchange load 10 454 7.5 3 4 17 0.00 % mixed-load mixed load 50 6,605 72.1 4 62 197 0.00 % saturation-1 auth stress, THINK=0 200 578,564 4,120 13 43 69 0.57 % saturation-4 auth stress, THINK=0 200 387,296 2,697 14 88 166 0.00 %

All scenarios with pauses (1–4) stayed within the SLO (errors < 1 %, p95 < 500 ms, p99 < 1.5 s).

docs.title: What the numbers show
docs.text:
1. Token cache (Redis) — Auth leaves the path. With the cache on, Prometheus recorded 7,571 hits and 21 misses in gateway_token_cache_total during the run: 99.7 % of validations did not call Auth (the 21 misses are ≈ 1 per test user). Without cache, all ≈ 7,400 requests went through POST /auth/solve. Latency dropped from p95 12 → 7 ms (−42 %). Throughput is the same in both runs because the pace is set by the users' pauses, not by the server.

2. Quote cache — the external API leaves the path. Without cache, every quote went to AwesomeAPI: p50 of 23 ms and p95 of 49 ms, the latency of a third-party service. With the 30 s cache, p50 of 3 ms and p95 of 4 ms (−92 %). At 10 users the external API held up without 429, but the volume of calls to it drops from ≈ 7 per second to 1 every 30 s per replica — that is what protects against the rate limit.

3. Replicas under "realistic" load — one gateway is plenty. With the pause between actions, 400 users generate ≈ 290 req/s, and a single replica answers with p95 of 3 ms. The differences between 1, 2 and 4 replicas (3 / 17 / 7 ms) are noise from freshly started JVMs (JIT not yet warmed up), neither gain nor loss. Honest conclusion: at this load the gateway is not the bottleneck; the reason to have 2+ replicas is availability (one can go down), not capacity.

4. Saturation — we found the real bottleneck, and it was not the gateway. Without pauses, the platform exceeded 4,100 req/s with one gateway replica, but 0.57 % of requests failed (3,279), all on GET /auth/me, none on GET /accounts/{id}. The gateway returned 500 and the Auth log showed exactly 3,279 × java.net.BindException: Cannot assign requested address:

flowchart LR
    gw[gateway] -->|"GET /auth/me"| auth[Auth]
    auth -->|"Feign: 1 new TCP connection<br/>per call (no pool)"| acc[Account]
    auth -.-x|"ephemeral ports<br/>exhausted → 500"| acc

Auth's GET /auth/me calls Account via OpenFeign with the default HTTP client, without a connection pool: each request opens a new TCP connection, and at 4,000 req/s the local ports of the Auth container run out (closed ones stay in TIME_WAIT). With 4 gateway replicas the machine was busier (CPU at ≈ 83 % in both runs, 4 JVMs competing for the same cores), throughput dropped to 2,697 req/s and Auth did not reach the limit — hence 0 errors, but twice the p95.

Suggested fix (Auth — Nicolas)

Replace the Feign client with one that has a connection pool and keep-alive — add io.github.openfeign:feign-hc5 to auth-service and spring.cloud.openfeign.httpclient.hc5.enabled=true. With reused connections, Auth stops opening one port per request. Then rerun ONLY=5 ./scripts/load-matrix.sh to confirm the 500s are gone.

5. Real usage (mixed). Within the SLO, but with the longest tail of the batch (p95 62 ms, p99 197 ms): 5 % of the actions are POST /auth/login, which hashes the password (expensive on purpose) and issues the JWT.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Everything on the same machine: k6 competes for CPU with the platform. The numbers show trends and bottlenecks, not the EKS capacity. On separate nodes, more replicas should increase throughput — here they were stuck on the same CPU.
  • Short runs (1–3 min) and one execution per configuration: differences of a few ms are noise.
  • 20 reused accounts: favors the token cache (it is the logged-in usage pattern, but a test with thousands of new users would have more misses).

To measure real capacity: BASE_URL=http://<elb> ./scripts/load-test.sh from another machine.

docs.title: EKS test with HPA
docs.text:
The course asks for a video of the load test running with the HPA scaling. Plan for the EKS run: k6 running from a member's machine against the ELB, and the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler creating gateway replicas when average CPU exceeds 50 % of the request (250m → 125m per pod).

Before you start

  • kubectl 1.36 or newer (kubectl version --client): the cluster is 1.37 and kubectl is only supported within one version of skew. The --cpu=50% in terminal 1 does not exist before 1.34 (unknown flag: --cpu).
  • metrics-server installed in the cluster (EKS does not ship it, and eks-store.yaml does not install it; without it the HPA stays at <unknown>). Install and check: kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml and, after ≈ 1 min, kubectl top nodes.
  • auth scenario, not exchange or mixed: AwesomeAPI returned 429 to the AWS IP, so Exchange answers 503 on EKS (mixed has 15 % exchange: that would give ≈ 15 % errors). With exchange on BACEN's PTAX (Exchange) the exchange rate no longer depends on AwesomeAPI, but PTAX is a public service: only with the cache on, no load testing against it.
  • Nobody pushes to main during the recording: the CI deploy runs kubectl apply on the gateway manifest (replicas: 2) and fights with the HPA.
  • Capacity: the 2 fixed nodes have room for ≈ 6 more gateway replicas (math in Costs), 8 in total. With --max=10, replicas 9 and 10 would stay Pending. The plan uses --max=6 to leave headroom: the spare capacity is split between the 2 nodes (≈ 0.8 vCPU on each) and a pod cannot use pieces of different nodes, so the 7th and 8th may not fit. If the group prefers to show the limit, use --max=10 and the Pending pods become part of the result.
  • More than one take: before repeating the test, kubectl rollout restart deployment/auth deployment/account -n store. In the rehearsal, Auth was killed for running out of memory on the second heavy run in a row (finding).

Three terminals side by side (Windows has no watch; kubectl's -w does the same):

1 · HPA2 · Gateway pods3 · k6 
kubectl autoscale deployment gateway --cpu=50% --min=2 --max=6 -n store
kubectl get hpa gateway -n store -w
# --cpu=50% existe desde o kubectl 1.34, que descontinuou o --cpu-percent=50 (ainda aceito,
# com aviso); num kubectl 1.33 ou anterior, só o --cpu-percent=50 funciona

kubectl get pods -n store -l app=gateway -o wide -w

ELB=$(kubectl get svc lb -n store -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].hostname}')
# (opcional) métricas do k6 no Grafana do cluster: noutro terminal,
#   kubectl port-forward svc/prometheus 9090 -n store
#   (no Linux, com --address 0.0.0.0: senão o container do k6 não alcança o port-forward)
BASE_URL=http://$ELB PROMETHEUS_RW_URL=http://host.docker.internal:9090 \
  NAME=eks-hpa SCENARIO=auth PROFILE=load VUS=100 DURATION=4m THINK=0 ./scripts/load-test.sh

--min=2 because the gateway manifest already starts 2 replicas: with --min=1 the HPA would remove one right at the start of the video. The HPA checks CPU every 15 s and metrics-server lags up to ≈ 1 min, hence the 4 min plateau. After the test, the HPA waits 5 min without load before scaling down: you can keep recording and show it going back to 2.

Grafana screenshot during the test (Observability page): kubectl port-forward svc/grafana 3000 -n store, dashboard Store — plataforma. The panel "Réplicas no ar ao longo do tempo (HPA)" shows the scale-up and the return to 2; "Requisições/s por réplica" and "CPU por réplica" show the new replicas joining and sharing the load.

Recording without depending on a window: scripts/eks-hpa.sh does everything at once (EKS result). Under the hood, scripts/hpa-record.py (code) runs the three terminals above, records the video and takes the Grafana screenshots by itself (details in the local rehearsal):

pip install playwright imageio-ffmpeg pillow    # uma vez; usa o Edge instalado
python scripts/hpa-record.py --base-url http://$ELB --name eks-hpa --label "EKS (eks-store)"

What to expect (seen in the local rehearsal): the new replicas took ≈ 1.5 min to receive their share of the load (why); with keepalive_time 10s applied afterwards to lb, they should take ≈ 35–40 s. During scale-down, the removed pods show up as Error in terminal 2. That Error is exit code 143 (128 + SIGTERM), which the JVM returns when Kubernetes tells the pod to stop, checked in the pod's state.terminated.exitCode: it is not a failure.

Afterwards: delete the HPA (kubectl delete hpa gateway -n store) before deleting the cluster.

docs.title: Local rehearsal (kind)
docs.text:
The plan above was rehearsed on 12/11/2026, before the EKS day, on a kind cluster (Kubernetes inside Docker) set up to resemble eks-store and with the same manifests:

eks-store (EKS) Local rehearsal (kind) Kubernetes 1.37 1.37 Nodes 2 × t3.medium 2 workers with the allocatable of a t3.medium (1930m CPU, 3.4 GiB) Manifests k8s/ and each service's k8s/ the same; only the image changes (the one from docker compose build) Database RDS Postgres inside the cluster Ingress ELB → lb localhost:8081 → lb NodePort HPA metrics-server metrics-server

The capacity math in Costs held up: with the platform running, each node had 1050m of CPU reserved out of 1930m, i.e., 3 more gateways fit per node (+6 in total). The rehearsal does not reproduce EKS latency (kind nodes share the machine's 12 cores, so a node can exceed 2 vCPU) nor the path through the internet and the ELB.

docker compose build              # imagens dos serviços
./scripts/kind-up.sh              # cluster + plataforma (≈ 4 min)
python scripts/hpa-record.py      # HPA + k6 + vídeo + prints do Grafana (≈ 11 min)
kind delete cluster --name store

hpa-record.py runs the three commands from the plan and shows the outputs side by side on a local page, which a windowless Edge captures twice per second: the video does not depend on an open window and shows nothing from the screen of whoever runs it. After k6 finishes, it keeps recording until the HPA is back to 2 replicas and saves to load/results/<nome>/ the video (real time and 8×), the replica timeline, a summary and the Grafana screenshots for the exact test interval.

docs.title: Rehearsal result
docs.text:
Run VUs Requests req/s p50 (ms) p95 (ms) p99 (ms) Errors Replicas (start → max) kind-hpa 100 435,094 1,606.5 48 148 196 0.00 % 2 → 6 Time since k6 start What happened 0 → 20 s k6 ramps from 0 to 100 VUs (auth scenario, no pause between requests) +27 s average gateway CPU at 131 % of the request (target: 50 %): the HPA asks for 4 replicas +40 s 4 replicas up and CPU at 206 %: the HPA asks for 6, the maximum +64 s all 6 replicas ready; none was left without room on the nodes (Pending) +75 s → +150 s the new replicas gradually start receiving load (finding) +4 min 33 s k6 finishes: 0 errors in 435,094 requests +10 min the HPA goes back to 2 replicas, ≈ 5.5 min after the load ends (the default wait is 5 min)

Video 8× faster (1 min 20 s for 10 min 36 s of test); the clock in the top-right corner shows real time. Terminal 1: the HPA (average CPU × target and replicas); terminal 2: the gateway pods being born (Pending → ContainerCreating → Running) and, at the end, leaving; terminal 3: k6. The real-time version is at load/results/kind-hpa/hpa-tempo-real.mp4 (17 MB, not in git).

Cluster Grafana during the test (from k6 start to the end of the load):

The dashboard's exchange row is empty because the auth scenario does not call the exchange service.

docs.title: Finding: new replicas take ≈ 1.5 min to receive load
docs.text:
The Requisições/s por réplica panel (stacked bands, one per replica) showed what k6 alone does not: the 4 replicas the HPA created were ready at +64 s, but received 0 req/s until ≈ +75 s and only shared the load evenly at ≈ +150 s.

Time since k6 start 2 old replicas (req/s each) 4 new replicas (req/s each) +60 s ≈ 740 0 +90 s ≈ 520 60 – 100 +120 s ≈ 360 175 – 340 +150 s ≈ 255 210 – 380

CPU shows the other side: the 4 new replicas start at 85–97 % of 1 CPU while receiving almost no requests (that is the JVM warming up: class loading and compilation), while the 2 old ones carry the load at ≈ 60–70 %. Only around +140 s do they all settle at ≈ 30–40 %.

Why: lb (Nginx) talks to the gateway Service, which is a virtual IP, and reuses connections (keepalive 32 in the upstream). The Service balances connections, not requests: each new connection is randomly assigned to a pod, but an open connection stays on the pod where it was created. The new replicas only receive new connections and, with steady load, Nginx only opens a new connection when it closes an old one, which by default happens after 1000 requests on the same connection (keepalive_requests). With ≈ 100 parallel requests and ≈ 1,600 req/s, each connection does ≈ 16 req/s and takes ≈ 1 min to reach 1000. It does not happen in compose because there Nginx sees each replica through Docker DNS and splits the requests itself.

Possible fixes (k8s/lb.yaml, Leonardo): fix 1 was applied after the rehearsal, so the EKS test already runs with it.

  1. One line in upstream gateways: keepalive_time 10s; (Nginx ≥ 1.21.3). Each connection lasts at most 10 s, so the new replicas join the split much earlier. Tested in the rehearsal, in two 3 min runs: the load was evenly split ≈ 35–40 s after the new replicas became ready, versus ≈ 86 s without the line, and the run with freshly restarted Auth and Account finished with 0 errors. Throughput from these runs is not comparable (in one, Auth went down, as in the finding below; in the other, Auth and Account had just restarted).
  2. Same as compose: a headless Service (clusterIP: None) for the gateway and, in Nginx, server <service-headless>:8080 resolve; with resolver kube-dns.kube-system.svc.cluster.local valid=10s;. Nginx then sees each pod and splits the requests itself, as in compose.

docs.title: Finding: Auth was OOM-killed in the following run
docs.text:
In the comparison run above (the second heavy run in a row), Auth was OOMKilled (code 137) at +3 min: during the next ≈ 30–40 s, while it restarted, the gateway got connection refused and connect timeout from Auth and returned 500 for 0.52 % of requests (1,413 failures, all on GET /auth/me).

The cause is in the Dockerfile of the four Java services: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75. With Auth's 512 Mi limit, the heap can reach 384 Mi, leaving only 128 Mi for the rest of the JVM (metaspace, threads, compiled code), too little for Spring Boot under load. The first run grew the heap and the second went over the limit. Account, with the same configuration, was at 393 Mi out of 512 Mi.

  • On EKS: between video takes, restart Auth and Account (kubectl rollout restart deployment/auth deployment/account -n store).
  • Suggested fix (Nicolas): -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60 (heap up to ≈ 307 Mi, ≈ 205 Mi for the rest) or a 768 Mi limit in Auth's and Account's k8s.yaml. The request, which is what the scheduler reserves, does not change, so the capacity math in Costs still holds.

docs.title: EKS result
docs.text:
Two runs on 19/11/2026, with the cluster up, in the auth scenario without pauses, for 4 min, with k6 running outside AWS (in Brazil) against the ELB:

Run VUs Requests req/s p50 (ms) p95 (ms) p99 (ms) Errors Replicas (start → max) eks-hpa (with HPA, recorded) 100 149,160 532.7 153 254 356 0.00 % 2 → 6 eks-auth-200 (no HPA) 200 230,602 819.4 193 370 630 0.00 % 2 (fixed)

Errors is k6's http_req_failed: the fraction of HTTP requests that failed (unexpected status or connection error), measured only in the test phase. The 0.00 % refers to HTTP requests, not pods.

eks-hpa was recorded with scripts/hpa-record.py by someone who had kubectl access to the cluster. eks-auth-200 ran only k6, from Gabriel's machine, which has no cluster access: without the HPA, the gateway stayed at the manifest's 2 replicas.

eks-hpa timeline (since the start of the load; the recorder's summary counts ≈ 19 s more, the time k6 took to pull the image):

Time What happened 0 → 20 s k6 ramps from 0 to 100 VUs +35 s average gateway CPU at 118 % of the request (target: 50 %): the HPA asks for 4 replicas +52 s 4 replicas up and CPU at 144 %: the HPA asks for 6, the maximum +91 s all 6 replicas ready, 3 on each node; none was left without room (Pending): the --max=6 capacity math held up on EKS +4 min 31 s k6 finishes: 0 errors in 149,160 requests +10 min the HPA goes back to 2 replicas, ≈ 5.5 min after the load ends

Video 8× faster (1 min 22 s for 11 min of test) on EKS; the clock in the corner shows real time. The new pods are born on both eks-store nodes (ip-10-20-…us-east-2.compute.internal) and, during scale-down, leave as Error (the JVM's code 143, see above). The real-time version (19 MB) is in load/results/eks-hpa/, not in git.

Cluster Grafana during the test (from the start of the load to the end of k6):

What the numbers show:

  • Within the SLO in both runs: p95 of 254 and 370 ms (< 500 ms), p99 of 356 and 630 ms (< 1.5 s) and 0 errors in 379,762 requests. Auth did not go down.
  • Latency is almost entirely network. With 1 user (smoke test before eks-auth-200), each request already took ≈ 180 ms: that is the round trip from Brazil to us-east-2. That is why throughput on EKS is lower than in the local rehearsal: the limit is how many round trips each user can make, not the server. To measure the cluster's capacity, k6 would have to run inside AWS.
  • Load balancing kept up with the new replicas: in the "Requisições/s por réplica" panel, the bands of the 4 replicas created by the HPA appear and grow while k6 runs. In eks-auth-200, 23 samples of /health-check through the ELB split 54 % / 46 % between the 2 replicas.
  • CPU repeats the rehearsal: the new replicas start at 60–85 % (the JVM warming up) and, once the load is split, all stay between ≈ 15 and 30 %.

Room for improvement: gateway graceful shutdown

During the scale-down from 6 to 2 replicas, 2 old gateway pods ended in Error (0/1) in terminal 2 of the video: it is the JVM's code 143 (SIGTERM), not an application failure, and the scale-down happened after k6 finished, so no request was lost in this run. But shutdown was not tested with traffic, and the gateway configures nothing for it: today the pod may stop while still receiving requests from Nginx. Proposed fix for the gateway:

  • server.shutdown: graceful and spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 20s in Spring Boot, to finish in-flight requests before exiting;
  • lifecycle.preStop with a sleep 5 and terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30 in the Deployment, so the pod leaves the Service (and Nginx) before the JVM receives SIGTERM;
  • repeat the scale-down with k6 running and check for 0 errors in that phase too.

To repeat the run: ./scripts/eks-hpa.sh (code) checks the prerequisites above (kubectl 1.34+, eks-store context, metrics-server, ELB responding; DRY_RUN=1 to only check), restarts Auth and Account and runs hpa-record.py. At the end, scripts/fill-eks-hpa.py builds the table row and the timeline from load/results/<nome>/resumo.json (measured numbers only) and prints the Markdown snippet to paste into this section.

docs.title: Code
Account
docs.text:
Owner: Nicolas · Repositories: pna26/account (interface) and pna26/account-service (implementation)

Account owns the store's account registry. It:

  1. creates, lists, fetches and deletes accounts (/accounts);
  2. stores the password only as a hash (the password is never saved or returned);
  3. checks email and password at login, on Auth's request (POST /accounts/login);
  4. records an AccountCreated event in the outbox, in the same transaction as the account, so the notification-service sends the welcome email.

It is a Spring Boot (Web MVC) + Spring Data JPA service on PostgreSQL, with the schema created by Flyway. It follows hands-on 1 of the course (and the login route from hands-on 3).

flowchart LR
    gw[gateway] -->|"/accounts/**<br/>+ id-account"| acc[account]
    auth -->|"Feign<br/>POST /accounts and /accounts/login"| acc
    acc -->|JPA| db[("PostgreSQL<br/>accounts schema")]
    acc -.->|"outbox → Kafka"| k[["account-events"]]

docs.title: Two repositories: interface and implementation
docs.text:
As in the course, each Java service has two repositories:

Repository Contents Used by account AccountController (interface with the routes, annotated with @FeignClient) and the DTOs AccountIn and AccountOut account-service (implements it) and auth-service (calls it) account-service the implementation: AccountResource, AccountService, JPA, Flyway, Dockerfile and k8s/ becomes the account-service image

The interface is published as a Maven library (store:account:1.0.0). This way the contract lives in one place: AccountResource implements AccountController, and Auth uses the same interface as a Feign client (http://account:8080). If a route changes, both sides stop compiling until they are updated.

docs.title: Routes
docs.text:
Method Route Input Output POST /accounts { name, email, password } 201 + Location: /accounts/{id} GET /accounts — [{ id, name, email }] GET /accounts/{id} — { id, name, email } or 404 DELETE /accounts/{id} — 204 POST /accounts/login { email, password } { id, name, email } or 401 (internal, called by Auth) GET /accounts/health-check — 200

Through the gateway, every /accounts/** route requires the token cookie. To create an account without being logged in, the path is Auth's POST /auth/register, which calls POST /accounts.

Status When 400 empty password or fewer than 6 characters; empty email 401 login with wrong email or password 404 GET /accounts/{id} for an id that does not exist 500 email already registered (see Limitations)

docs.title: Sign-up flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as auth
    participant R as AccountResource
    participant S as AccountService
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    A->>R: POST /accounts {name, email, password}
    R->>S: create(Account)
    S->>S: validates password (≥ 6) and email
    S->>S: hash = Base64(SHA-256(password))
    S->>DB: BEGIN
    S->>DB: INSERT accounts.accounts
    S->>DB: INSERT accounts.outbox (AccountCreated)
    S->>DB: COMMIT
    R-->>A: 201 Location: /accounts/{id}

Login takes the reverse path: it hashes the received password and looks for an account with that email and that hash (findByEmailAndHashPassword). If none is found, it responds 401 without saying whether the error was in the email or the password.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text: Decision Reason Resource → Service → Repository layers, with Account (domain), AccountModel (JPA) and AccountParser Course pattern. The JPA entity never leaves the service and the output DTO (AccountOut) has no password field, so the hash cannot leak by mistake. UUID id generated by JPA The id reveals neither how many accounts exist nor the sign-up order. email with UNIQUE in the database The "one email, one account" rule holds even with several account replicas creating at the same time. accounts schema (not public) created by Flyway Each service has its own schema in the same PostgreSQL (notification uses notification). Migrations are versioned in the repository and run automatically at boot, including on RDS. 404 when the id does not exist The client can tell "account does not exist" apart from a server error. 401 on wrong login, without saying whether the email or the password was wrong Does not help anyone trying to find out which emails are registered. Auth forwards it as 401. Account and event in the same transaction (@Transactional) This is the messaging transactional outbox: if the account INSERT fails (duplicate email), the event is rolled back too. Database and Kafka via environment variables The same jar runs in compose (db), on local Kubernetes and on EKS (RDS endpoint in the ConfigMap, username and password in the account-secrets Secret).

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Behaviors that came from the course code and were left as they are. They are part of what we would explain for a production version:

Limitation How it would look in production Unsalted SHA-256 hash: two accounts with the same password have the same hash BCrypt or Argon2 (deliberately slow and salted), for example Spring Security's PasswordEncoder Duplicate email returns 500 handle the DataIntegrityViolationException and return 409 Conflict Any logged-in user can list and delete any account (GET /accounts, DELETE /accounts/{id}) authorization by role or resource owner: compare the gateway's id-account with the route's {id}, or require an admin role POST /accounts/login also goes through the gateway (with token) keep the route on the internal network only, like /auth/solve

Configuration
